title: Learn Spring Boot for Back-end development
description: Start your backend development journey with Spring Boot, a powerful Java-based framework designed to simplify building production-grade applications. Learn the core concepts like RESTful APIs, dependency injection, and application configuration, and see how to connect with databases using JPA and Hibernate. As you progress, dive into real-world features like validation, error handling, and layered architecture. Perfect for Java beginners, this hands-on path helps you move from writing simple endpoints to building complete backend systems — all with minimal setup and maximum productivity.

modules.title: Spring Boot Fundamentals
modules.description: This module covers the basics of Spring Boot, a powerful framework that simplifies Java application development. Learn the difference between Spring and Spring Boot, the idea of convention over configuration, and how to handle XML/JSON, use Hibernate/Spring Data JPA, and manage dependencies with Maven. You’ll also build your first Spring Boot app, understand @SpringBootApplication, and run it using main() or mvn spring-boot:run.

pages.title: Welcome to the Spring Boot Course!
pages.content:
- Are you ready to dive into the world of backend development with **Spring Boot**, one of the most powerful and widely-used Java frameworks?
- In this course, you’ll go from zero to building **real-world REST APIs** and **secure, layered web applications** using modern Spring Boot practices.

---

**Why Learn Spring Boot?**

- Spring Boot is one of the **most in-demand backend technologies** in the industry.
- It **allows** you to build **scalable, secure, and production-ready applications** faster and easier than traditional Java frameworks.
- Whether you want to become a backend developer, full-stack developer, or build your own products, Spring Boot gives you the power to do it.
- **No prior backend experience is required** to get started.






**Get ready to start your backend development journey** — click **Next** to begin the course.

pages.title: Spring and Spring Boot
pages.content:
Let’s say you’re building a Java app, like a simple **Student Management System**. \
**You create classes like:**
- `StudentService` → contains the logic
- `StudentRepository` → talks to the database

Now comes the boring part: \
You need to **manually create objects**, connect them, and make sure everything runs smoothly. It works — but it gets messy fast.

---

**How Spring Helps**
- Spring acts like a **smart assistant** for your Java app.
- Instead of you doing everything yourself, **Spring says**:
```sss
“Just tell me what you need.
I’ll create the objects and connect them for you.”
```
**You don’t create objects manually** anymore — **Spring handles** it.

**Spring does this using two superpowers:**
- **IoC (Inversion of Control)** – Spring controls object creation, not you
- **DI (Dependency Injection)** – Spring gives each class what it needs

Don’t worry — we’ll explain this in detail later in the course.

---

**Core Idea**
- Spring is a **tool that takes care of object creation** and **connections** so you can focus on writing logic.
- That’s why companies love Spring. It’s fast, clean, and powerful.

pages.title: Introduction to Spring Boot
pages.content:
Spring is super helpful… but setting up a Spring project used to feel like **setting up a tent without instructions**:

* You had to **configure everything** manually
* Add a bunch of **XML files or annotations**
* Decide which **dependencies** to include (and manage them yourself)

**In short:** 
It was powerful, but also **complicated & hard to get started with**. 

---

**This is where Spring Boot helps** : \
Spring Boot was created to make things simple and fast. Instead of struggling with spring setup.



---

So… **What is Spring Boot?**

**Spring Boot** is like a **pre-configured version of Spring** that helps you:

* Gives you a ready-to-use project
* Configures things automatically (so you don’t have to configure everything)
* Lets you start coding immediately
* Run your app with a single command
* Focus on writing business logic — not setup

---

**Real-life analogy**

- Let’s say Spring is a **DIY furniture kit** — all the parts are there, but you need to assemble them.
- Spring Boot is the **same furniture — but already assembled**, tested, and ready to use.
- You just unbox it, plug it in, and go.

practiceProblems.title: Spring Initializr Setup
practiceProblems.description:
By now, you know:
- **Spring** → helps manage your Java objects and their dependencies
- **Spring Boot** → simplifies Spring by handling setup and configuration automatically. 

At this point, you might be thinking : \
**“Okay… but how do I actually start a Spring Boot project?”**

**That’s where Spring Initializr comes in.**

---

**What is Spring Initializr :** \
**Spring Initializr** is a simple **website that generates a ready-made Spring Boot project** for you. \
You don’t have to:
- Create folders yourself
- Configure files manually
- Set up everything from scratch \
It does the hard work for you. 

---

**How to Set Up a Project Using Spring Initializr**
1. Open **Spring Initializr** in your browser: https://start.spring.io/
2. Select:
- Project: **Maven**
- Language: **Java**
- Packaging: **Jar**
- Java Version: **17**
3. Add dependency: **Spring Web**
4. Click **Generate** to download the project.
5. **Extract the ZIP** and open it in your IDE.
Your setup is done!

**Take a look at the visualizer given here to see how all the project options are displayed**

---

In this course, your Spring Boot project setup is already done in your lab environment. \
This explanation of **Spring Initializr** is just to **help you understand how projects are created** in the real world — no manual setup needed.

pages.title: Understanding Your Spring Boot Project Structure
pages.content:
Now that you have created your first Spring Boot app, let’s slow down and understand what exactly is inside the project and how Spring Boot works behind the scenes.

---

**Project Structure Overview**
```jsx
workspace/
 └── demo/
 └── src/
 └── main/
 ├── java/
 └── resources/
```

---


**Let’s break this Project Structure :**

- **`src/main/java` → Your Application Code** \
This is where all your Java code lives.
Inside it, you will find:
```sss
src/main/java/com/example/demo/
 HelloController.java ← your controllers
 DemoApplication.java ← main class
```
Think of this folder as the “brain” of your application. \
Your **controllers, services, repositories, configuration files** — everything goes here.

---


- **`src/main/resources` → Your App Settings + Templates + Static Files** \
Contains important resources used by your application:
```sss
src/main/resources/
 application.properties ← app settings (port, DB config, etc.)
 static/ ← CSS, JS, images for web apps
 templates/ ← HTML templates (if using)
```

pages.title: When You Run a Spring Boot Application
pages.content:
When you run your Spring Boot application, several things happen automatically in the background. You don’t have to manually control them.

---

**1. Maven prepares and runs your project**

Maven is a project helper tool (similar to **npm** in Node.js).

It helps by:

* Reading a file called `pom.xml` (this file tells Maven what your project needs)
* Downloading required libraries automatically
* Compiling your Java code
* Running your Spring Boot application

So instead of doing all this manually, Maven does it for you.

---

**2. Spring Boot starts your application**

Spring Boot:

* Finds the main class marked with `@SpringBootApplication`
* Starts the application from there
* Sets up everything your app needs
* Creates the Spring environment (also called Spring Context)

You don’t need to configure all this yourself.

---

**3. Built-in web support starts automatically**

- Your Spring Boot app can run in a browser because it includes built-in web support (the built-in web server is called Tomcat).
- You do NOT need to: Install a server, Configure a server
- This happens because of this dependency in `pom.xml`:

```xml

 org.springframework.boot
 spring-boot-starter-web

```

This tells Spring Boot: This is a web application and it should run in a browser

practiceProblems.description:
- Let's see the working of first springboot application.

---

**How to Run the App**

You have two options to run the project:

1. **Click the “Run” button** (in your editor or provided interface)
2. Or open the terminal and run:

```bash
cd ~/workspace/demo
mvn spring-boot:run
```

This will launch the application and you'll see **“Hello, From Spring Boot!”**.

---

**How the Code Works :**
- The application starts from the `main()` method in `DemoApplication.java`.
- Spring Boot automatically starts a web server in the background.
- While starting, Spring scans the project and finds `HelloController`.
- `@GetMapping("/")` tells Spring which method should run when a request comes in.
- Spring calls the `home()` method.
- The method returns a text message.
- Spring sends this text back as the response.

That’s how **“Hello, From Spring Boot!”** appears in the browser.

---

**Quick Note About Project Setup**

- Normally, you can go to [https://start.spring.io](https://start.spring.io) to create a Spring Boot project from scratch. \
But **for this problem**, we’ve already created and given you a **basic Spring Boot starter project**, which:
* Is configured with **Spring Web** dependency
* Has all the folder structure ready
* Includes a **pre-written controller** for you to explore

---

This is the magic of Spring Boot: **easy startup with minimal configuration.**

pages.title: Introduction to API
pages.content:
Before we dive into building APIs…
Have you ever thought about this? 

**How does data actually come to your app?**
- You click buttons every day.
- You see data on screens all the time.
- But how does that data arrive there?

**Let’s find out by using a demo API first.**

---

**Open your browser and type this URL:**
```sss
https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1
```
Press `Enter`. \
**You will see something like this:**
```json
{
 "id": 1,
 "name": "Leanne Graham",
 "email": "leanne@example.com"
}
```
This **format** is called **JSON**.

**You just made an API call.** \
There was no login page and no buttons or screens — just data returned directly by a server. \
**This is exactly how an API works.**

---

**What just happened?**
- You typed a URL
- The browser sent a request
- Some server sent back data
- The data came in JSON format

**This data response is the result of an API call.**

pages.title: What Is an API (Application Programming Interface)
pages.content:
Imagine you go to a restaurant. 
- **You** are the customer (**User**/**Frontend**)
- **The chef(kitchen)** prepares the food (**backend**/**server**)
- **The waiter** takes your order to the chef and brings the food back to you (the **API**)

You never walk into the kitchen or talk to the chef directly. The waiter handles all communication between you and the kitchen.

---

In an application, an API works like the **waiter** in a restaurant.

Just like you don’t go into the kitchen or talk to the chef directly, an app or user never talks to the backend or database directly. **The API stands for Application Programming Interface that takes the request from the app, passes it to the backend (the chef), and then brings the response back**.

In simple words, **an API is a way for one application to communicate with another application**.

pages.title: How the Request - Response flow works
pages.content:
You’ve already seen how a restaurant works — you place an order, the waiter communicates with the kitchen, and the food comes back to you. \
Now let’s use that same example to understand how **requests and responses** work in applications.

---

**When you place an order in a restaurant:**

1. You place the order
2. The waiter takes it to the kitchen
3. The chef prepares the food
4. The waiter brings the food back to you


**The same idea applies to applications.**

1. The app sends a request
2. The API forwards the request to the backend
3. The backend processes it
4. The API sends back a response




---

**Key takeaway** \
Every time you see data on your screen, this request → response flow has already happened. \
The **API** is the **middle layer** that makes this communication possible.

This is the exact flow you will implement when you start building APIs using **Spring Boot** in the next section.

practiceProblems.title: Spring Boot API Demonstration - Sending JSON
practiceProblems.description:
**Look at the given code in your IDE**. You can see that the `getUser()` method returns some data in the form of a Map. \
Don’t focus on `@GetMapping` or `@RestController` for now. \
**Let’s first understand what JSON is and how APIs use it**.

---

When you run this API and access the endpoint, the output looks like this:
```json
{
 "id": "1",
 "name": "Leanne Graham",
 "email": "leanne@example.com"
}
```

This is **JSON**, a standard format APIs use to **exchange data** between servers and clients (like web browsers, mobile apps, or other services).

---

**What is JSON?**
- **JSON** = JavaScript Object Notation
- A **lightweight, human-readable format** for data
- Structured with **key-value pairs**, like a Java Map
- Here, In JSON output :
 - `"id"`, `"name"`, `"email"` → keys
 - `"1"`, `"Leanne Graham"`, `"leanne@example.com"` → values
 - Values can also be numbers, arrays, or nested objects

---

**How APIs Use JSON**
1. **Sending Data (Response)**
- API sends JSON to clients (browser, app, etc.)
- Example: our `/` endpoint **returns the user info in JSON**

2. **Receiving Data (Request)**
- APIs can also accept JSON from clients
- **Example client request:**
```json
{
 "name": "Jane Doe",
 "email": "jane@example.com"
}
```

**The API will read this JSON and perform actions, like saving the data to a database.** \
We’ll cover this in detail next.

practiceProblems.title: Spring Boot API Demonstration - Receiving JSON
practiceProblems.description:
**APIs are not just for sending data**; they can also **receive data from clients**.

In this lab, your **API can accept JSON data**, which is a structured way to send information over the internet. 
**Example client request** (JSON):
```json
{
 "name": "Jane Doe",
 "email": "jane@example.com"
}
```
Give your name and email in JSON format, **Click on `Send JSON`**, You'll get **Response**. 

The client (like a web page, Postman, or another application) sends this data to your API. \
The API reads the JSON automatically and converts it into a Java object behind the scenes.

---

Don’t worry about the Java code here. \
**The key is to understand the data flow**:
```sss
Client → JSON → Spring Boot API → Java Object → Response
```

**Right now, your API is configured to**: 
1. Read the JSON sent by the client.
2. Convert it to a Java object (`UserRequest`).
3. Print it in the console so you can see the data arrived successfully.
4. Return a confirmation message to the client (Response).

Later in the course, **this object can be used to save data to a database or perform other actions**.

pages.title: Understanding the GreetingController Code
pages.content:
Let’s now understand the controller code you used in the previous lab and see **how it handles incoming requests**.

**GreetingController.java**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/greet")
public class GreetingController {
```
**What This Class Does**
- `GreetingController` is a **controller class**
- It is **responsible for handling HTTP requests**
- All API logic for greeting messages is written inside this class
- This is where Spring Boot looks when a request comes in.


**`@RestController`** \
Tells Spring Boot this class **handles API requests** and **sends responses** directly (usually in JSON format), instead of rendering a web page..

**`@RequestMapping("/api/greet")`** \
Tells Spring Boot to send all requests starting with `/api/greet` to this class.

---

**Handling a Simple GET Request** \
Code :
```java
@GetMapping("/hello")
public String helloWorld() {
 return "Hello, World!";
}
```

**`@GetMapping("/hello")`** \
Runs this method when `/api/greet/hello` is called.

---

In this lab, you learned **how to create a GET API using Spring Boot**. \
You used `@GetMapping` to map URLs to methods, returned responses from the API, and tested the endpoints. 

In the next section, you will practice creating GET APIs on your own.

**Try It Yourself :** 
1. Run the application. 
2. The **Greeting API Tester** will open automatically. 
3. Enter the URL below, click **`Call API`**, and observe the response.

**URL :**
```java
/api/greet/hello
```
**Response:**
```sss
Hello, World!
```

**Congratulations! You just interacted with a real API.**


---

**Now the Question: How Did This Work?** \
When you typed a URL:
- Your browser sent a request
- Spring Boot received that request
- A specific class handled it
- A method returned a response

That **class** is called a **Controller**. 

---

**What Is a Controller in Spring Boot?** \
A Controller is a class in Spring Boot that:

- Listens for **incoming HTTP requests**
- Decides **what code should run**
- Sends a **response back to the client**

In simple words:
```sss
Controller = Traffic controller for URLs
```
Whenever a request comes in, the controller tells Spring: \
**“For this URL, run this method.”**

---


**Note** : \
For now, just run the application, enter the URL, and observe the output. \
Don’t worry about `@RestController`, `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping` yet — we will understand these step by step later.

practiceProblems.title: Building Your First GET API
practiceProblems.description:
Imagine you are building an app that manages users. Your app needs to send user information to other parts of the app or even other applications. 

In this demo, we created a `UserController` with several endpoints to:
- Get individual users (Alice, Bob, Charlie)
- Get a list of all users

This is exactly how real-world APIs work—you request data from a URL, and the server sends it back as JSON. 

---

**Before we begin** :
1. Run the application.
2. The API Tester will open automatically.
3. **Enter below URL** one by one -> Click on **"Call API"** and **Observe the Resopnse**

```java
/api/users/alice
/api/users/bob
/api/users/charlie
/api/users/all
```

**Let’s break down how this code works step by step**.

---

**How the Code Works**

**1. Class-level annotations**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
```

- `@RestController` → Marks the class as a controller for APIs.
- `@RequestMapping("/api/users")` → Sets a base URL for all APIs in this controller. \
Every method in this class will start with `/api/users`.

---

**2. Single user endpoints**
```java
@GetMapping("/alice")
@GetMapping("/bob")
@GetMapping("/charlie")
```

`@GetMapping` maps a specific URL → method.

**Examples:**
- `/api/users/alice` → calls `getAlice()` → returns Alice’s info
- `/api/users/bob` → calls `getBob()` → returns Bob’s info
- `/api/users/charlie` → calls `getCharlie()` → returns Charlie’s info

---


**3. List of users endpoint**
```java
@GetMapping("/all")
public List getAllUsers()
```
- Returns a list of User objects.
- Spring Boot automatically converts **Java objects → JSON array**.

Example URL: `/api/users/all` → Returns:

```json
[
 { "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com" },
 { "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com" },
 { "name": "Charlie", "email": "charlie@example.com" }
]
```

pages.title: GET vs POST
pages.content:
Till now, you have worked with both GET and POST APIs in Spring Boot.
This section is a quick and clear recap to reinforce what you already practiced.

Now let’s clearly understand how they are different and when to use which.

---

**What is the purpose?**



---

**How is data sent?**

**GET API**
- Data is sent as part of the request URL
- The client requests information using a URL

**POST API**
- Data is sent in the request body
- Usually in JSON format

---

**Spring Boot Annotations**
```sss
GET =	 @GetMapping
POST =	 @PostMapping
```

**Simple rule to remember**
- If you are getting data → use **GET**
- If you are sending data → use **POST**

---

Now that you know how requests work, 
let’s learn how Spring Boot receives input data.

practiceProblems.title: Building Your First POST API
practiceProblems.description:
Imagine you are building an app to **manage users**. You want to let clients (frontend apps, Postman, etc.) **add new users** to your system.

In this demo, we created a **UserController** with an endpoint to:
- Add a single user

This is exactly how real-world APIs work — **you send JSON to a URL, the server receives it, stores it, and responds with a confirmation message**.

Note: There is also a **GET endpoint** available to see which users have been added for your better understanding, but **we will not focus on GET here**.

---

**Before we begin** :

1. Run the application.
2. The API Tester will open automatically.
3. Send JSON to the following URLs and observe the response:

**Example Request**

1. POST – Add single user
```sss
POST : /users
```

```json
{
 "name": "David",
 "email": "david@example.com"
}
```

**Response:**
```sss
"User added successfully!"
```

---

**How the Code Works**

- **Single user POST endpoint**
```java
@PostMapping
public String addUser(@RequestBody User user) {
 users.add(user);
 return "User added successfully!";
}
```
- `@PostMapping` → Maps the URL /users to this method.
- `@RequestBody` → Converts incoming JSON into a Java User object automatically.
- `users.add(user)` → Adds the user to the in-memory list.
- `Return message` → Sends a confirmation string back to the client.

---

**Key Points**
- POST APIs → Used to send data to the server.
- `@RequestBody` → Automatically converts JSON → Java objects. \
We'll see `@RequestBody` later in detail.

**For Testing :** \
After sending your `POST` request, you can select **`GET`** and type **`/users` in your API tester*** to see whether your user has been added successfully.

pages.title: Handling Input Data in Spring Boot
pages.content:
Now that you have practiced GET and POST APIs, you know how a client can call an API to fetch or send data. \
But in real applications, APIs don’t work alone — they also need to **accept input data from the client**.

This input data can come in **different ways**, such as:
- Values inside the **URL**
- Values sent as **query parameters**
- Data sent as **JSON in the request body**

---

To handle these different inputs, **Spring Boot provides three important annotations**:

1. **@PathVariable** – \
used when data comes from the **URL path**

2. **@RequestParam** – \
used when data comes from **query parameters**

3. **@RequestBody** – \
used when data comes from the **request body** (JSON)

Let’s see when and why to use each of these annotations — one by one.

pages.title: PathVariable
pages.content:
`@PathVariable` is used when **input data is part of the URL itself**. \
The value is written directly in the URL path and Spring Boot extracts it and passes it to the method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@PathVariable` when:
- You want to **identify a specific resource**
- The value is **mandatory**
- The URL clearly represents what you are accessing

**Example URL:**
```java
/api/users/101
```
- Here, `101` is a **input value** passed directly in the URL.
- It Extracts values from the URL
- Passes them to the controller method

**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @GetMapping("/{id}")
 public String getUserById(@PathVariable int id) {
 return "Fetching user with id: " + id;
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**

`{id}` → placeholder in the URL \
`@PathVariable int id` → captures the value from the URL \
`Calling /api/users/101` → id becomes $101$

---

**Common use cases:**
- Fetching a user by ID
- Deleting or updating a specific record

pages.title: RequestParam
pages.content:
`@RequestParam` is used when **input data is sent as query parameters in the URL**. \
The value is written after the `?` symbol in the URL and Spring Boot reads it and passes it to the method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@RequestParam` when:
- The input value is **NOT part of the main URL path**
- The value is often optional
- The data is used for **filtering, searching, or sorting**
- The URL represents an **action**, **NOT** a specific resource

**Example URL:**
```java
/api/users?role=admin
```
- Here, `role` is an **input value passed as a query parameter**
- It Extracts values from query parameters
- Passes them to the controller method



**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @GetMapping
 public String getUsersByRole(@RequestParam String role) {
 return "Fetching users with role: " + role;
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**
- `?role=admin` → query parameter in the URL
- `@RequestParam String role` → captures the value from the URL
- Calling `/api/users?role=admin` → role becomes `admin`

---

**use cases:**
- Searching users by name or role
- Filtering results
- Sorting data

pages.title: RequestBody
pages.content:
`@RequestBody` is used when input data is sent **inside the request body** (usually as JSON). \
Spring Boot reads the request body, converts the JSON into a Java object, and passes it to the controller method.

---

**When do we use it?** \
Use `@RequestBody` when:
- You are sending **complex data** (objects, multiple fields)
- Data is coming from a **POST / PUT request**
- Input is **not suitable for the URL**
- You want to send data securely and cleanly

**Example Request Body (JSON):**
```json
{
 "name": "Alice",
 "email": "alice@example.com"
}
```
This data is sent **inside the body**, not in the URL.


**What does it do?**
- Reads data from the HTTP request body
- Converts JSON → Java Object
- Passes the object to the controller method



**Controller Code (Demo)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {

 @PostMapping
 public String addUser(@RequestBody User user) {
 return "User added: " + user.getName();
 }
}
```

**What’s happening here?**
- `@RequestBody User user` → captures JSON from request body
- JSON fields are mapped to the `User` class
- Spring Boot handles conversion automatically

---

**Common use cases:**
- POST & PUT HTTP methods - commonly used with `@RequestBody`
- Creating a new user
- Submitting forms
- Sending login or registration data
- Updating records with multiple fields

This API allows the user to **enter an API URL** and sends a **GET** request to the backend.

---

---

**Your Task :** \
Create a Spring Boot controller that:
- Accepts text input from the URL query parameter
- Uses `@RequestParam` to read the input
- Converts the text to uppercase or lowercase
- Returns the converted text as the response.

---

**API Requirements**

```java

```

```java
GET /api/text/lowercase?text=value
```

---

**Each API should**:
- Accept the input using `@RequestParam`
- Read the value from the query parameter named `text`
- Return the converted text as the response

Start your Spring Boot application \
Once the application runs successfully, the API Tester page will open automatically in your browser

---

**Step 2: Test “Submit Feedback” POST API** \
In the API tester:
- Select **POST** as the **HTTP** method
- In the URL input field, type:
```sss
/feedback
```
In the request body section, enter JSON:
```json
{
 "username": "alice",
 "message": "Very easy to understand API example"
}
```
Click the `Send` button

**What happens:**
- The POST request is sent to the backend
- The feedback data is sent in **JSON format**
- `@RequestBody` reads the JSON data from the request body
- Spring converts the JSON into a `Feedback` Java object
- The feedback object is added to the in-memory list
- A success message is returned

---


**Step 3: Test “Get All Feedback” GET API** \
In the API tester:
- Select **GET** as the HTTP method
- In the URL input field, type:
```sss
/feedback
```
Click the `Send` button

**What happens:**
- The **GET** request is sent to the backend
- The controller fetches all feedback from the list
- The stored feedback is returned as a response

---

**For Testing:**

After sending your **POST** request, you can select **GET** and type **`/feedback`** in your API tester to check whether your feedback has been added successfully.

---


**Goal:** \
The goal of this exercise is to practice creating a POST API using `@RequestBody` in Spring Boot.

---

**Your Task:** \
Build a simple Support Ticket application. The application should allow clients (like frontend apps or Postman) to:
- Raise a new support ticket via **POST API** using `@RequestBody` to read JSON input.
- Fetch all tickets via **GET API** (for testing only).

Implement the **POST API** that will take a JSON object representing a **Ticket**, read it using @RequestBody, and store it in an in-memory list.

---

**Example JSON for POST request:** 

Select **POST** and add the **JSON request**:
```json
{
 "ticketTitle": "Cannot login",
 "description": "I am unable to login to my account"
}
```

**After adding a ticket, the API should return a confirmation message like**:
```sss
"Ticket submitted successfully!"
```

---

**For Testing**: \
After sending your **POST** request, you can select **GET** and type **`/tickets`** in your API tester to check whether your tickets has been added successfully.

modules.title: Building a Feature
modules.description: In this module, you will build a simple Book Manager application using in-memory storage. You will create a List to store books, implement a POST API to add new books, and use GET APIs to retrieve all books or fetch a book by its ID. All the logic will be written inside the Controller, helping you clearly understand how CRUD operations work before moving to layered architecture.

practiceProblems.title: Practice Project - Build Book Manager API
practiceProblems.description:
**Instructions:**
1. **Complete your code** first.
2. Click on **"Run"** to **start the server** and make sure it runs correctly.
3. If you **make any changes** to the code after running, you must **run the server again**.
4. Only after running the server with the **latest changes**, your submission will reflect the updated solution.
5. **Do not submit** if the server is not running; otherwise, your solution will **fail**.


---



**Goal :** \
Create a simple **Spring Boot REST API** that manages books. \
You will build APIs that allow users to:
- Add a new book
- View all books
- View a book using its ID

This project helps you understand how basic APIs work in Spring Boot.

---

**Project Overview :** \
You are given a partially completed controller class for a Book Manager application. \
Some parts of the code are intentionally missing. \
Your task is to complete the code so that the API works correctly. \
The application will store books in memory using a list (no database required).

**Book Information** \
Each book should contain:
- `id` → unique number (generated automatically)
- `title` → name of the book
- `author` → author of the book

---

**Your Task :** \
Complete the missing parts in the template code by following the instructions written as TODO comments. \
You need to: 

**1. Create Storage for Books**
- Initialize an in-memory list to store books.
- Create a variable that helps generate unique IDs.

**2. Complete the Book Class** \
Inside the controller, complete the Book class by adding:
- id field
- title field
- author field

**3. Implement Add Book API** \
Complete the method that:
- Receives book data from request body
- Assigns a unique ID to the book
- Adds the book to the list
- Returns the saved book

**Endpoint**
```sss
POST /api/books
```
**Example request body:**
```json
{
 "title": "Clean Code",
 "author": "Robert C. Martin"
}
```

**4. Implement Get All Books API** \
Complete the method that:
- Returns all stored books.

**Endpoint**
```sss
GET /api/books
```

**5. Implement Get Book By ID API** \
Complete the method that:
- Accepts an ID from the URL
- Searches the list for a matching book
- Returns the book if found
- Returns null if not found

**Endpoint**
```sss
GET /api/books/{id}
```

**Example:**
```json
GET /api/books/1
```

---

**Rules :**
- Do NOT use a database.
- Everything should remain inside one controller.
- Use only an in-memory List.

pages.content:
- You are working on the same application from the previous page.
- Currently: An order is placed, Payment is done using Credit Card

--- 

**Now the business introduces a new requirement:** The application should support UPI payments. Later, more payment methods may be added.

- You are asked to update the existing code to support this requirement.
- A new payment class is available:

```java
class UPIPaymentService {
 public void pay() {
 System.out.println("Payment done using UPI");
 }
}
```


The rest of the application remains unchanged.

---


**To support UPI payments without removing Credit Card payments, the following changes were made:**
 - A new UPIPaymentService class was added
 - OrderService now creates both payment service objects
 - Conditional logic (if-else) is used to decide which payment method to use at runtime

This solution allows the application to support multiple payment methods at the same time, and it works correctly.

**However, an important design issue still exists.**

practiceProblems.title: Loose Coupling Demonstration
practiceProblems.description:
Run the given code and understand how the code works and how it solves the tight coupling problem we saw earlier.

**1. Role of `PaymentServiceInterface`**
```java
public interface PaymentServiceInterface {
 void pay();
}
```

This interface represents **any type of payment.**
- `OrderService` depends on this interface
- It does not depend on any specific payment implementation

This is the key step that **removes tight coupling.**

**2. Payment Implementations**
```js
class CreditCardPaymentService implements PaymentServiceInterface { ... }
class UPIPaymentService implements PaymentServiceInterface { ... }
```
**Each payment type:**
- Implements the same interface i.e `PaymentServiceInterface`
- Provides its own implementation of `pay()`

**New payment methods can be added by creating new classes that implement the interface**.

**3. `OrderService` (Loose Coupling)**
```java
public class OrderService {
 private PaymentServiceInterface paymentService;

 public OrderService(PaymentServiceInterface paymentService) {
 this.paymentService = paymentService;
 }

 public void placeOrder() {
 paymentService.pay();
 System.out.println("Order placed");
 }
}
```

**Here:**
- `OrderService` does not create payment objects
- It receives the dependency from outside 
- It only knows about the interface, not the concrete class

**This is what makes the design loosely coupled.**

**4. Main Class (Dependency Injection)**
```java
PaymentServiceInterface payment = new UPIPaymentService();
OrderService orderService = new OrderService(payment);
```

**Here:**
- The payment method is chosen in `Main`
- The selected payment object is passed into `OrderService`
- This is manual Dependency Injection using Traditional Java Approach

---


**Your Task** \
Open file : `Main.java` \
Currently, the application uses UPI:
```java
PaymentServiceInterface payment = new UPIPaymentService();
```
**Change it to Credit Card**:
```java
PaymentServiceInterface payment = new CreditCardPaymentService();
```
**Run the application again and observe the output.**

**Expected Output**
```sss
Payment done using Credit Card
Order placed
```

practiceProblems.title: Practice - Loose Coupling
practiceProblems.description:
You’ve seen how `OrderService` uses `PaymentServiceInterface` to place an order without worrying about the payment method. \
Currently, our code has two payment methods:
- `CreditCardPaymentService` → prints: "Payment done using Credit Card"
- `UPIPaymentService` → prints: "Payment done using UPI"

The `OrderService` does not need to change when we switch payment methods. This is **loose coupling in action**.

---

**Your Task :**

**Step 1 — Create a New Payment Method in `PaymentMethods.java`**
- Create a new class called `PayPalPaymentService`.
- Make it implement `PaymentServiceInterface`.
- Implement the `pay()` method to print:
```sss
Payment done using PayPal
```
Note : To create new class `PayPalPaymentService` - You can take reference from other classes present in `PaymentMethods.java` 

**Step 2 — Update `Main.java`** 
- Change the line where `CreditCardPaymentService` is used
- Replace it with your new service `PayPalPaymentService`
- Do NOT change `OrderService.java`
- After your change, `Main.java` should use your new payment method.

**Step 3 — Run the Code**
- When you run `Main.java`, the **expected output should be**:
```sss
Payment done using PayPal
Order placed
```

---

Notice how the order service didn’t change at all, but we can now process payments using a completely new method. \
**That’s the power of loose coupling!**

practiceProblems.title: Problem with Loose Coupling
practiceProblems.description:
- Using interfaces, we improved the design and made `OrderService` loosely coupled.
- This is a good design. But look at how the application starts(main function).

We are still **manually creating and selecting objects**.

---

**What Is the Issue?**

As the application grows:

* More payment methods are added
* More `if-else` logic is needed
* Startup code becomes large and messy

Object creation logic spreads across the codebase and becomes hard to manage.

---

**Key Idea:** The problem is no longer design, but **manual object management**.

We need a way to:

* Create objects automatically
* Inject the correct dependencies
* Avoid writing wiring code ourselves

This is exactly what **Spring Boot Dependency Injection** provides.

pages.title: Beans & Annotations
pages.content:
Now that we’ve seen how the order and payment flow works in previous example, it’s important to understand the main Spring components that made this possible. These are the building blocks Spring uses to manage objects, dependencies, and the application itself. 

---

**What is beans:**
- In Spring, a bean is simply an **object that Spring manages for you**.
- Instead of manually creating objects with `new`, **Spring creates, manages, and provides these objects wherever they are needed**.
- Beans are the building blocks of a Spring application — **services, repositories, controllers, or other components** can all be bean.

---

**In previous example, we have the following annotations:**
1. **`@Service`**
- Marks a class as a **service bean** (business logic).
- Spring automatically creates an object (bean) of this class.

2. **`@Primary`**
- **Marks a bean as the default** when multiple implementations of an interface exist.

3. **`@Autowired`**
- Tells Spring to automatically inject a bean (object) into a class.
- Spring finds the matching bean and provides it — no `new` keyword needed

4. **`@Override`**
- Java annotation
- Marks that a method overrides a method from an interface or parent class.

5. **`@SpringBootApplication`**
- Marks the **main class** of a Spring Boot application — this is the starter of your app.

---

pages.title: ApplicationContext - The Brain Behind Beans
pages.content:
You learned about Beans and Annotations:
- What a bean is?
- How annotations like `@Service`, `@Autowired`, and `@Primary` work?
- That Spring creates objects for us instead of using `new`?

**Now a very important question arises:** 
```sss
Who creates these beans? 
Who keeps track of them? 
Who injects one bean into another? 
```
**The answer is ApplicationContext.**

---

**What is ApplicationContext?** \
ApplicationContext is the **Spring container**. \
It is the core object in Spring that:
- Creates beans
- Stores beans
- Injects beans into each other
- Manages the application lifecycle

**Think of it like** \
You already know: \
`@Service` → tells Spring this class should be a bean \
`@Autowired` → tells Spring inject a bean here

But **Spring itself needs a manager to make this happen** - That manager is **`ApplicationContext`**.

---

**What Exactly Does ApplicationContext Do?** \
When the application starts, ApplicationContext: \
**1. Scans the project** \
Looks for annotations like `@Service`, `@Component`, `@Controller` \
**2. Creates Beans** \
Creates objects of all detected beans \
**3. Stores Beans** \
Keeps them in memory \
**4. Injects Dependencies** \
Handles `@Autowired` \
Injects the correct bean automatically \
**5. Manages Lifecycle** \
Controls when beans are created and destroyed

pages.title: The Solution - Layered Architecture
pages.content:
To solve this problem, Spring Boot follows a **layered architecture**.
The idea is simple: **split responsibilities instead of putting everything in one place**.

This concept is called **Separation of Concerns** — each part of the application focuses on one specific job.

---

**Standard Layers:**
```java
Controller → Service → Repository
```
- **Controller :** \
Handles **HTTP requests** and **responses**. \
It does not contain **business logic**.

- **Service Layer :** \
Contains **business logic** \
Decides **what should happen** \
**Coordinates** between **controller and repository** 

- **Repository Layer :** \
Handles **data access** and storage \
Manages **data operations** \
**Stores** and **retrieves** data \
**Communicates with the database**

---

**Let's understand this layered architecture visually**



**Request Flow:**

```java
Client → Controller → Service → Repository → Database
Database → Repository → Service → Controller → Client
```

Each layer has **one clear responsibility**, making the application easier to understand, test, and maintain. 

---

In the next sections, **we’ll refactor our application step by step using this layered approach**.

pages.title: Understanding Layered Architecture (From Task API)
pages.content:
In the previous practice, you converted a working API into a Layered Architecture. \
Now let’s clearly understand:
- What each layer does
- How they communicate
- How Spring connects everything automatically
- How a request flows step by step

---

**What is Layered Architecture?** \
Layered Architecture means:
- Dividing an application into different layers
- Each layer has a specific responsibility
- No layer should do everything

In our Task API, we followed this flow:
```sss
Controller → Service → Repository
```
Each layer has one clear job.

---

**Let's Understand Code Properly :** \
**`DemoApplication.java` (Application Start)**
```java
@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {

 public static void main(String[] args) {
 SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
 }
}
```
**What this does :**
- Starts the Spring Boot application.
- Spring scans the project and finds classes marked with:
 - `@RestController`
 - `@Service`
 - `@Repository`
- Spring automatically creates objects of those classes and connects them together.

This is why we never write `new TaskService()` manually.

---

**`TaskRepository.java` (Data Storage)**
```java
@Repository
public class TaskRepository {

 private final List tasks = new ArrayList<>();
}
```
**What this does**
- **`@Repository` tells Spring this class manages data**.
- Spring creates one shared object of this class.
- tasks list works like a small in-memory database.

**Saving data**
```java
public void save(String title) {
 tasks.add(title);
}
```
**What happens**
- Receives a task title.
- Adds it into the list.
- This is where data actually gets stored.

**Getting data**
```java
public List findAll() {
 return tasks;
}
```
**What happens**
- Returns all stored tasks.
- No logic — just gives stored data.

**Repository = only store & fetch data**.

---


**`TaskService.java` (Middle Layer)**
```java
@Service
public class TaskService {

 private final TaskRepository taskRepository;
}
```
**What this does**
- `@Service` tells Spring this class contains application logic.
- Service needs Repository to access data.

**Dependency Injection** (Important)
```java
public TaskService(TaskRepository taskRepository) {
 this.taskRepository = taskRepository;
}
```

**What happens**
- Spring automatically sends the repository object here.
- We did NOT create it manually.

**Meaning:**
```sss
Spring creates Repository
 ↓
Gives it to Service
```
This is called **Dependency Injection (DI)**.


**Adding a task**
```java
public void addTask(String title) {
 taskRepository.save(title);
}
```
**What happens** :
- Controller calls this method.
- Service forwards task to repository for saving.
- Service itself does not store data.

**Getting all tasks**
```java
public List getAllTasks() {
 return taskRepository.findAll();
}
```
**What happens**
- Service asks repository for stored tasks.
- Returns them back to controller.

**Service = middle communicator**.

---

**`TaskController.java` (API Layer)**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/tasks")
public class TaskController {

 private final TaskService taskService;
}
```
**What this does**
- `@RestController` → handles HTTP requests.
- All APIs start with `/api/tasks`.
- Controller needs Service to perform work.


**Dependency Injection again**
```java
public TaskController(TaskService taskService) {
 this.taskService = taskService;
}
```
**What happens**
- Spring gives Service object to Controller automatically.
- Flow now becomes connected:
```sss
Controller → Service → Repository
```

**POST API (Add Task)**
```java
@PostMapping
public String addTask(@RequestBody String title) {
 taskService.addTask(title);
 return "Task added successfully!";
}
```

**What happens step-by-step**
- User sends POST request.
- Spring reads request body into title.
- Controller calls service:
```java
taskService.addTask(title);
```
- Service sends data to repository.
- Repository stores it in list.
- Controller returns success message.

**GET API (Get Tasks)**
```java
@GetMapping("/list")
public List getTasks() {
 return taskService.getAllTasks();
}
```
**What happens**
- User requests task list.
- Controller asks Service.
- Service asks Repository.
- Repository returns stored list.
- Response goes back to user as JSON.

---

**Full Flow When API runs:** 

```sss
Client Request
 ↓
TaskController
 ↓
TaskService
 ↓
TaskRepository
 ↓
List (data stored)
```
Response comes back the same way.

**One Simple Rule** \
Controller never directly accesses data. \
Always:
```sss
Controller → Service → Repository
```

pages.title: Problem in Current Layered Design
pages.content:
Right now, our classes depend directly on **concrete implementations**. \
**In Previous Example, You've seen:**
```java
public class NoteService {

 private final NoteRepository noteRepository;

 public NoteService(NoteRepository noteRepository) {
 this.noteRepository = noteRepository;
 }
}
```
**Here:**
- `NoteService` directly depends on `NoteRepository`
- The service **knows exactly which repository implementation is used**
- This creates **tight coupling**.


**What is Tight Coupling?** \
Tight coupling means: \
One class is strongly dependent on a specific implementation of another class.

---

**Real Problem Example** \
Today we are using:
- In-Memory Repository (ArrayList)

**Tomorrow we may want:**
- Database repository (MySQL/PostgreSQL)
- File storage
- External API storage

If `NoteService` depends directly on `NoteRepository`, we must modify existing code whenever implementation changes.

This breaks an important clean architecture principle: \
**High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules.**

---

**Solution — Interface-Based Design** \
Instead of depending on a class, we depend on a contract. \
That contract is called an **Interface**.

**An interface defines :** \
What operations are available \
**NOT :** \
How they are implemented

---

Let’s see this practically in the next section -

practiceProblems.title: Interface-Based Notes API - Demo
practiceProblems.description:
Now we’ll convert your **Notes API** into **Interface-Based Design** using proper layered architecture. \
We will create:
```json
Controller → Service (interface + impl) → Repository (interface + impl)
```
This is the **standard Spring Boot industry structure**.

---

**How Project Structure looks in this Example:**
```sss
com.example.demo
│
├── controller
│ └── NoteController.java
│
├── service
│ ├── NoteService.java (INTERFACE)
│ └── NoteServiceImpl.java (IMPLEMENTATION)
│
├── repository
│ ├── NoteRepository.java (INTERFACE)
│ └── InMemoryNoteRepository.java (IMPLEMENTATION)
```

---

**1. NoteRepository (Interface)**
```java
public interface NoteRepository {
 void save(String note);
 List findAll();
}
```
**What this code does :**
- This is a repository contract.
- It defines the operations related to data storage.
- It does not contain any implementation logic.

**Methods**
- `save(String note)` → used to store a note
- `findAll()` → used to retrieve all notes

Any repository class must implement these methods.

---

**2. InMemoryNoteRepository (Repository Implementation)**
```java
@Repository
public class InMemoryNoteRepository implements NoteRepository {
```
**What this class does**
- Provides the **actual implementation** of the repository interface.
- Stores notes using an in-memory list.

**In-memory storage**
```java
private final List notes = new ArrayList<>();
```
- Creates a list to store notes temporarily.
- Data exists only while the application is running.

**Save method**
```java
@Override
public void save(String note) {
 notes.add(note);
}
```
Adds the received note into the list.

**Fetch method**
```java
@Override
public List findAll() {
 return notes;
}
```
Returns all stored notes.

**Annotation :**
```java
@Repository
```
- Marks this class as a repository component.
- Spring automatically creates and manages its object.

---

**3. NoteService (Interface)**
```java
public interface NoteService {
 void addNote(String note);
 List getAllNotes();
}
```
**What this code does**
- Defines business operations related to notes.
- Contains only method declarations.
- No logic is written here.

**Methods**
- `addNote()` → adds a note
- `getAllNotes()` → retrieves notes

---

**4. NoteServiceImpl (Service Implementation)**
```java
@Service
public class NoteServiceImpl implements NoteService {
```
**What this class does**
- Contains the **business logic** of the application.
- Uses repository methods to perform data operations.

**Dependency declaration**
```java
private final NoteRepository noteRepository;
```
- Service depends on the repository interface.
- The actual implementation is injected by Spring.

**Constructor Injection**
```java
public NoteServiceImpl(NoteRepository noteRepository) {
 this.noteRepository = noteRepository;
}
```
- Spring automatically provides a repository object.
- No manual object creation is required.

**Add note logic**
```java
@Override
public void addNote(String note) {
 noteRepository.save(note);
}
```
Calls repository to store the note.

**Get notes logic**
```java
@Override
public List getAllNotes() {
 return noteRepository.findAll();
}
```
Retrieves notes from repository.

**Annotation**
```java
@Service
```
- Marks this class as a service layer component.
- Spring manages its lifecycle automatically.

---

**5. NoteController**
```java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/notes")
```
**What this class does**
- Handles HTTP requests.
- Communicates with the service layer.
- Does not contain business or storage logic.

**Service dependency**
```java
private final NoteService noteService;
```
Controller uses the service interface.

**Constructor Injection**
```java
public NoteController(NoteService noteService) {
 this.noteService = noteService;
}
```
Spring injects the service implementation automatically.


**POST Endpoint — Add Note**
```java
@PostMapping
public String addNote(@RequestBody String note)
```
- Receives note text from request body.
- Calls service to add the note.
- Returns success message.

**GET Endpoint — Get Notes**
```java
@GetMapping("/list")
public List getNotes()
```
- Calls service to fetch all notes.
- Returns notes as JSON response.

practiceProblems.title: Building Your First User CRUD
practiceProblems.description:
Our UserController is a REST API for managing users. All endpoints start with the base URL:
```java
/api/users
```
Each HTTP method does a specific operation — this is the CRUD pattern:
- **C → Create** → POST
- **R → Read** → GET
- **U → Update** → PUT
- **D → Delete** → DELETE

Let’s go through each endpoint. \
**1. Create (POST)** \
Endpoint:
```sss
POST /api/users
```
Since you already know POST, we won’t spend too much time here. It creates new data.

---

**2. Read (GET)** \
Two Endpoints here:
```sss
GET /api/users -> Get all users (Returns a list of all users.)
GET /api/users/{id} -> Get user by ID (Returns a single user by its ID.)
```
You already know GET — it retrieves data.

---

**3. Update (PUT)** \
Annotation Used:
```java
@PutMapping("/{id}")
```

Endpoint:
```ss
PUT /api/users/{id}
```

**What it does:**
- Updates an existing user by ID.
- Requires the ID in the URL and a JSON body with updated information, e.g.:
```sss
{
 "name": "Bob"
}
```

**Controller Code:**
```java
@PutMapping("/{id}")
public String updateUser(@PathVariable int id,
 @RequestBody Map user) {

 if (id >= 0 && id = 0 && id < userService.getUserCount()) {
 userService.deleteUser(id);
 return "User deleted successfully!";
 } else {
 return "User not found!";
 }
}
```

**What happens:**
1. ID is taken from URL
2. It checks if ID exists
3. If valid → calls:
```java
userService.deleteUser(id);
```
4. Returns success message
5. If invalid → returns:
```sss
"User not found!"
```
6. So this deletes one specific user.


**Response**: \
`"User deleted successfully!"` or `"User not found!"`.

---

- **Delete all users** \
Annotation:
```java
@DeleteMapping
```

```sss
DELETE /api/users
```
Clears the entire user list.

**Controller Code:**
```java
@DeleteMapping
public String deleteAllUsers() {
 userService.deleteAllUsers();
 return "All users deleted successfully!";
}
```
**What happens:**
- No ID required
- Calls:
```java
userService.deleteAllUsers();
```
- Clears the entire list
- Returns success message


**Response:** \
 `"All users deleted successfully!"`

**Hello Developers!** Welcome to the **Note-Taking API Project** 

In this project, you will build a **backend REST API** using **Spring Boot** that allows users to manage personal notes. \
Modern backend systems are built using clean architecture, where responsibilities are clearly separated. \
This project is designed to help you understand how a real backend application works internally-from handling HTTP requests to managing data in memory.

Chef wants a lightweight backend service where users can:
- *Create notes*
- *View all notes*
- *Update existing notes*
- *Delete notes*

Your task is to complete the missing logic and make the API fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given 4 Java files representing a **Layered Architecture**:
- `Note.java` → Model class
- `NoteController.java` → REST Controller
- `NoteService.java` → Service layer
- `NoteRepository.java` → Repository layer (in-memory storage)

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names

practiceProblems.title: URL Shortener Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Learners!** Welcome to the **URL Shortener Project** 

In this project, you will build a **backend REST API** using Spring Boot that converts long, messy URLs into short, clean, and shareable links.

Sharing long web addresses can be cumbersome. Chef needs a high-performance, lightweight service where users can shorten URLs and, when they click the short link, be instantly redirected to the original website.

Your **task** is to **complete the missing logic** and make the API fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **4 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
1. `UrlRequest.java` → Model class (Data Transfer Object).
2. `UrlRepository.java` → Repository layer (In-memory storage using HashMap).
3. `UrlService.java` → Service layer (Business logic & Hashing).
4. `UrlController.java` → REST Controller (API Endpoints).

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with `TODO`
- The testing system relies on the existing structure
- **In-Memory Storage:** Data is stored in a `HashMap`. Data is lost when the application restarts (this is expected behavior).

**Data Structure** \
You will be working with two primary structures in this project:
1. **The Request Object (Input):**
 - `originalUrl` (String) - The long URL provided by the user that needs to be shortened (e.g., `https://www.codechef.com/`).
2. **The Storage Map (Internal Memory):**
 - **Key** (String): The generated `shortCode` (e.g., `"5d4140"`).
 - **Value** (String): The `originalUrl` associated with that code.
 - *Note:* This Map acts as your temporary database.

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Model** \
 **File:** `model/UrlRequest.java` This class is the "envelope" that holds the data sent by the user.
 - **Constructor:** Complete the **Parameterized Constructor**. Assign the passed variable (`originalUrl`) to the class field.
 - **Encapsulation**: Implement the missing **Getters** and **Setters** so other classes can access and modify the private data. \
**Docs:** How JSON Maps to Java Objects

2. **Build the Repository (The Database Layer)** \
 **File:** `repository/UrlRepository.java` This class manages the raw data in a HashMap.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Repository.
 - **`saveUrl` Method:** Store the mapping in the `urlStore` map. Use the `shortCode` as the Key and `originalUrl` as the Value. 
 - **`getOriginalUrl` Method:** Retrieve the original url from the map using the `shortCode`.
 - **`exists` Method:** Return `true` if the map contains the `shortCode`, otherwise return `false`.
 - **`getAllUrls` Method:** Return the entire map. \
**Docs:** @Repository Annotation | Java HashMap | Java Map Interface (put, get, containsKey)

3. **Connect the Service (The Logic Layer)** \
 **File:** `service/UrlService.java` This class handles the logic, specifically generating the unique hash.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Constructor Injection:** Initialize the `urlRepository` variable inside the constructor.
 - **`shortenUrl` Method:**
 - **Hashing:** We use MD5 to generate a unique code. Use `DigestUtils.md5DigestAsHex` on the original URL bytes (Code provided).
 - **MD5 (Message-Digest Algorithm 5)** is a cryptographic hash function that converts any input (like a long URL) into a fixed-length 32-character hexadecimal string.
 - Hashing is **one-way**, meaning you can’t reverse it to get the original URL - perfect for generating unique, consistent codes.
 - In this project, we use Spring’s built-in `DigestUtils` class to create an MD5 hash of the long URL and then take the **first 6 characters** of that hash as the `shortCode`.
 - Substring: Extract the **first 6 characters** of the generated hash to create the `shortCode`.
 - Logic: Check if the code already exists in the repository. If it does **NOT**, save the new mapping.
 - Return: Return the generated `shortCode`.
 - **`getOriginalUrl` Method:** Call the repository to fetch the URL. \
**Docs:** Spring Constructor Injection | @Service Annotation | MD5 Hashing in Java | Java substring() Method

4. **Define the API Endpoints (The Controller Layer)** \
 **File:** `controller/UrlController.java` This class talks to the outside world (Frontend/Postman).
 - **Constructor:** Inject the `UrlService` into the controller.
 - **Endpoint 1:** Create Short URL
 - **Goal:** Receive a long URL and return a short code.
 - **Annotation:** Use `@PostMapping` and map it to `"/api/shorten"`.
 - **Input:** The method should accept a `@RequestBody` of type `UrlRequest` (code provided).
 - **Logic:**
 1. Extract the original URL from the request object.
 2. Call `urlService.shortenUrl(...)` to generate the code.
 - **Response:**
 - Wrap the result in a `ResponseEntity` (code provided).
 - Return a JSON Map where the key is `"shortCode"` and the value is the code you generated.
 - Example Output JSON: `{ "shortCode": "5d4140" }`
 - **Endpoint 2:** Redirect to Original URL
 - **Goal:** When a user visits the short link, redirect them to the real website.
 - **Annotation:** Use `@GetMapping` and map it to `"/{shortCode}"`. 
 - **Input:** Use `@PathVariable` to capture the `shortCode` from the URL.
 - **Logic:**
 - Call `urlService.getOriginalUrl(...)` to find the long URL.
 - Check: If the URL is `null` (not found), return a **404 Not Found** status (code provided).
 - Success: If found, return an **HTTP 302 (Found)** status.
 - **Important:** You must set the **Location Header** of the response to the **original URL** so the browser knows where to go. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | @RequestBody Annotation | @PathVariable Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | HTTP 302 Found (Redirect) | HTTP 404 Not Found

---

**Expected Behaviour:** \
Since our CodeChef domain itself is a little long, the generated short URLs you see here may also appear slightly longer than typical short URLs.

practiceProblems.title: Encryption Terminal Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Innovators!** Welcome to **Project 1: Encryption Terminal** 

In this project, you will build a **Spring Boot Backend** that acts as a digital coding machine. It converts readable text into secret codes and back again. \
**Data security is important!** Chef needs a secure way to transmit messages so that no one else can read them. Your system will use a classic **Caesar Cipher** algorithm to "shift" letters. 

Your **task** is to **complete the missing backend logic** to make this terminal fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **3 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
1. `EncryptionResponse.java` → **Model** (Data Transfer Object) that structures the JSON output.
2. `EncryptionService.java` → **Service** (Business Logic) that handles the math and string manipulation.
3. `EncryptionController.java` → **Controller** (API Endpoints) that handles web requests.

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

---

**The Logic: Caesar Cipher** \
This project uses a simple substitution method called the **Caesar Cipher**.
- **The Key:** We use a SHIFT of **5**.
- **Encryption:** Every letter moves **forward** by 5 spots in the alphabet (e.g., `A` becomes `F`).
- **Decryption:** Every letter moves **backward** by 5 spots to reveal the original message.
- **Wrap-Around:** If you shift past 'Z', you go back to 'A'. This is done using **Modulo Arithmetic** (`%`).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Model** \
 **File:** `model/EncryptionResponse.java` This class acts as the "box" that holds the answer we send back to the user.
 - **Constructor:** Assign the incoming parameters (`originalText`, `transformedText`, `operation`) to the class fields.
 - **Getters:** Implement the methods to return the private field values so the system can convert them to JSON. \
**Docs:** Anatomy of a Java Class

2. **Connect the Service (The Brain)** \
 **File:** `service/EncryptionService.java` This is where the actual scrambling happens.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Process Method (The Loop):**
 - **Loop:** Convert the text to a char array and iterate through it.
 - **Base Logic:** Determine if the letter is Lowercase ('a') or Uppercase ('A') to select the correct base ASCII value (97 for 'a', 65 for 'A') needed to normalize the 0-25 index.
 - **The Math:** Apply the cipher formula using the `base` you just identified: `((character - base + shift) % 26) + base`
 - **Non-Letters:** In the `else` block (numbers, spaces, symbols), do **NOT** change the character. Append it directly to the result.
 - **Encrypt/Decrypt Methods:** \
 Call the private `process()` helper method, passing the correct shift value.
 - *Hint for Decrypt:* call the `process()` function with the input `text`. For the second argument, you must reverse the shift using this formula: `26 - (SHIFT % 26)`. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Java StringBuilder | ASCII Table

3. **Define the API Endpoints (The Controller Layer)** \
 **File:** `controller/EncryptionController.java` This class listens for requests from the outside world.
 - **Class Configuration:** Ensure this class is recognized as a **REST Controller** and handles requests starting with the base path `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Ensure the `EncryptionService` is correctly initialized via the constructor so the controller can use it.
 - **Endpoint 1: Encrypt a Message**
 - **Goal:** Create an endpoint that allows users to send plain text and receive the scrambled code. 
 - **Mapping:** This method should handle GET requests at the path `"/encrypt"`.
 - **Input:** The method expects a value to be passed in the URL query string (e.g., `?message=Hello`). Use the appropriate Spring annotation to bind this parameter to a String variable.
 - **Logic:** Pass the captured input to your service layer to generate the encrypted text.
 - **Response:** Create and return a new instance of your `EncryptionResponse` model. Ensure the operation type is set to `"encryption"`.
 - **Endpoint 2: Decrypt a Message**
 - **Goal:** Create an endpoint that allows users to reverse the process and recover their original text.
 - **Mapping:** This method should handle GET requests at the path `"/decrypt"`.
 - **Input:** Similar to the encryption endpoint, capture the message parameter from the URL.
 - **Logic:** Pass the captured input to your service layer to retrieve the original text.
 - **Response:** Create and return a new instance of your `EncryptionResponse` model. Ensure the operation type is set to `"decryption"`. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | Spring @RequestParam | Mapping Requests

---

practiceProblems.title: Mars Rover Navigator Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Learners!** Welcome to the **Mars Rover Navigator Project** 

In this project, you will build the **backend logic** for a navigation system that guides a rover across the surface of Mars. The rover moves on a grid, and your code will determine where it ends up based on a series of commands.

**Precision is key!** We need to ensure the rover stays within its exploration zone and doesn't drive off the map. Your system will track **Coordinates (X, Y)** and **Direction (N, E, S, W)**.

Your **task** is to **complete the missing backend logic** to make this navigation system fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **3 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
1. `Rover.java` → **Model:** A simple object (POJO) that holds the state (Position X, Position Y, and Direction).
2. `RoverService.java` → **Service** (Business Logic): The "Brain" that calculates turns, movement, and checks boundaries.
3. `RoverController.java` → **Controller** (API Endpoints): The "Doorway" that listens for web requests and talks to the service.

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

---

**The Logic: Navigation & Grid** \
This project uses a **2D Cartesian Grid** (10x10).
1. **The Grid:** Coordinates range from 0 to 9.
2. **Starting Point:** The rover always starts at (0, 0) (Bottom-Left corner).
3. **Default Direction:** North ("N").
4. **Turning**
 - **Left ('L'):** Rotates the rover 90 degrees Counter-Clockwise (e.g., North → West).
 - **Right ('R'):** Rotates the rover 90 degrees Clockwise (e.g., North → East). 
5. **Moving ('F')** \
Moves the rover **one step forward** in the direction it is currently facing.
 - **North:** Increases Y (moves up).
 - **South:** Decreases Y (moves down).
 - **East:** Increases X (moves right).
 - **West:** Decreases X (moves left).
6. **Safety Boundaries** \
The exploration zone is limited! The rover **cannot** move to a coordinate less than **0** or greater than **9**. If a command tries to push it off the edge, the rover must **ignore that move** and stay put.

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Model** \
 **File:** `model/Rover.java` This class represents the "body" of the rover. It remembers where it is.
 - **Constructor:** Initialize the `x`, `y`, and `direction` fields. The default constructor should set them to `0`, `0`, and `"N"`.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Implement the methods to allow other classes to read and modify these values. \
**Docs:** Anatomy of a Java Class

2. **Connect the Service (The Brain)** \
 **File:** `service/RoverService.java` This is where the magic happens.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Initialization:** Instantiate the `rover` object in the constructor so it is ready to use.
 - **Command Processing:** Implement the `processCommands(String commands)` method
 - This method should take a string of characters (e.g., `"FFR"`). 
 - Loop through each character and call the corresponding logic method (`turnLeft`, `turnRight`, or `moveForward`). 
 - Ignore any characters that are not `'F'`, `'L'`, or `'R'`.
 - **Reset Logic:** Implement the `resetRover()` method to snap the rover back to **(0, 0)** facing **"N"**.
 - **Turning Logic:** Complete the switch statements in `turnLeft()` and `turnRight()`.
 - *Hint:* If you are facing **North** and turn **Left**, you are now facing **West**.
 - **Movement Logic:** Complete the `moveForward()` method.
 - Check the **Boundary Condition** first! Only update the coordinate if the new position is valid (between 0 and 9). \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Java Switch Statements

3. **Define the API Endpoints (The Controller Layer)** \
 **File:** `controller/RoverController.java` This class receives commands from the outside world (the frontend).
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Ensure the `RoverService` is correctly assigned in the constructor.
 - **Endpoint 1: Get Status**
 - **Goal:** Retrieve the current coordinates and direction of the rover without moving it.
 - **HTTP Method:** Use **GET** because we are just reading data. 
 - **Path:** Map this to `"/status"` (Combined URL: `/api/status`). 
 - **Logic:** The Controller doesn't store data itself. **Ask your Service layer** to provide the current `Rover` object it is holding.
 - **Return:** The `Rover` object obtained from the service. Spring will automatically format it as JSON.
 - **Endpoint 2: Move Rover**
 - **Goal:** Accept a string of commands (e.g., `"FFR"`) and execute them.
 - **HTTP Method:** Use **POST** (since we are modifying the state).
 - **Path:** Map this to `"/move"`.
 - **Input:** The commands come in as a query parameter (e.g., `?commands=FF`). 
 - *Hint:* Use the `@RequestParam` annotation to capture this string.
 - **Logic:** The Controller is just a messenger. **Pass the captured command string** to the Service layer method responsible for processing movement logic.
 - **Return:** The updated `Rover` object returned by the service.
 - **Endpoint 3: Reset**
 - **Goal:** Send the rover back to the starting position (0,0).
 - **HTTP Method:** Use **POST** (since this is an action). 
 - **Path:** Map this to `"/reset"`.
 - **Logic:** Trigger the **method in your Service layer** designed to restore the rover to its default starting coordinates and direction.
 - **Return:** The `Rover` object, which should now reflect the starting position. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | @GetMapping & @PostMapping | Spring @RequestParam

---

**Expected Behaviour:**

modules.title: Database Integration with JPA
modules.description: This module introduces how to connect a Spring Boot application to a database using JPA. It explains the need for databases, basics of ORM, JPA, and the use of Hibernate and Spring Data JPA. You will learn to set up an H2 database, create entities, and use repositories for CRUD operations.

topics.title: Why Database & ORM
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Why Database & ORM.

pages.title: Why Database
pages.content:
**First, Let’s Connect to What You Already Built** \
Till now in your course:
- You built APIs 
- You created a Book Manager 
- You implemented Full CRUD 
- You used Layered Architecture & Interfaces 

But… \
Everything was stored **in memory (List)**.

---

Now think about this… \
**What happens if you restart your application?** -> All data disappears.

That’s the **real problem** -> **In-Memory Data is Temporary**

**That Means :** 
- Restart app, Data gone
- Server crash, Data gone
- Deploy to production, Data gone
- Multiple users, Not scalable

So for real-world applications, this is NOT acceptable. \
We need **permanent storage**.

Thus We Need a **Database**

---

**What is DataBase?** \
A database **stores data permanently**. \
Instead of storing data inside a List temporary, we store them inside a database table.

**Now:**
- Restart app - Data still there
- Thousands of users - Works
- Large data - Works
- Production ready - Yes

pages.title: What is ORM & Why We Need
pages.content:
Now Consider You're using Database - **But New Problem Appears…** \
Java works with:
- Classes
- Objects

Database works with:
- Tables
- Rows

---

**So how do we convert:**
```java
Book book = new Book("Spring", "John");
```
**into**


**Manually writing SQL** for everything would be **painful**. \
This is where **ORM comes in**.

---

**What is ORM?** \
ORM = **O**bject **R**elational **M**apping

It is a technique that:
```sss
Converts Java Objects ⇄ Database Tables automatically.
```
Simple meaning:
- Java class → Database table
- Object → Row
- Fields → Columns

So **instead of writing SQL manually, we work with Java objects**. \
**ORM handles database interaction** for us.

pages.title: Intro to JPA
pages.content:
Now you understand what ORM is...But here’s something important \
ORM is just a concept, It is not a library.

So the next question is:
**Who actually implements ORM in Java?**

This is where **JPA comes in**.

---

**JPA = Java Persistence API**
JPA is a specification. \
It is a set of rules that tells:
- How Java classes should map to database tables
- How objects should be saved and fetched
- How CRUD operations should work

Important:
- JPA is NOT a tool.
- JPA does NOT contain actual code to talk to the database.
- It just **defines the rules**.

Think of JPA like:
- A rule book for ORM in Java.
- But rule books alone don’t do the work.

We need someone to follow those rules and implement them

---

**So, To actually use JPA, we need an implementation**. \
The most popular implementation of JPA is:
- **Hibernate**

**Hibernate is the real engine that:**
- Generates SQL
- Creates tables
- Executes queries
- Talks to the database

So:
- JPA → Rules
- Hibernate → Does the actual work

When you use Spring Boot with JPA, **internally Hibernate is working for you**.

Next, Let'see - How this works practically from a simple demo example :

pages.title: Intro to Spring Data JPA
pages.content:
Now here comes the best part : \
Even Hibernate can require some boilerplate code. \
Spring Boot makes it even simpler using : **Spring Data JPA**

---

**With Spring Data JPA, you don’t:**
- Write implementation classes
- Write SQL for basic CRUD
- Write boilerplate code
- You just create an interface like this:
```java
public interface BookRepository extends JpaRepository {
}
```
And you automatically get:
- `save()`
- `findAll()`
- `findById()`
- `deleteById()`

Without writing any implementation \
**Spring generates everything for you at runtime**.

---

**Big Picture** \
Let’s connect everything clearly:
```sss
Database → Stores data
ORM → Concept to map objects to tables
JPA → Rules for ORM in Java
Hibernate → Implements JPA
Spring Data JPA → Makes Hibernate super easy to use
```

pages.title: What Just Happened Behind the Scenes
pages.content:
How JPA, ORM & Hibernate Work Together in previous book API example \
We created this class: `Book.java`
```java
@Entity
public class Book {
 @Id
 @GeneratedValue
 private Long id;
 private String title;
 private String author;
}
```
And we saved a book like this:
```java
bookRepository.save(book);
```

---

Now let’s understand what actually happens step by step:

**Step 1 — ORM Concept** \
**ORM means:**
```sss
Convert Java Object ⇄ Database Table
```
So:
- Book class → becomes a table
- Book object → becomes a row
- Fields → become columns

This is just the concept.

---

**Step 2: JPA Came Into Action** \
**When called:**
```java
bookRepository.save(book);
```
Spring Data JPA handled it. \
But Spring Data JPA does not directly talk to database. \
**It uses JPA.**

**JPA defines:**
- How this object should be mapped
- Which table it belongs to
- How `save()` should behave
- JPA gives the rules for mapping objects to database.

**Because of:**
```java
@Entity
public class Book
```
**JPA understood:**
- This class = Table
- This object = Row

---

**Step 3: Hibernate Did the Real Work** \
Hibernate implements JPA.

**Hibernate:**
- Reads Book object
- Converts it into SQL
```java
INSERT INTO book (title, author) VALUES (?, ?)
```
- Executes that SQL
- Returns saved object with generated ID

So Hibernate does the real database work.

---

**Step 4: H2 Database Stored It**
- H2 received the SQL query.
- It inserted the row into: BOOK table
- That’s why when you ran:
```java
SELECT * FROM BOOK;
```
You saw the data in table.

pages.title: Setting Up The Database (H2)
pages.content:
In the previous demo, you:
- Added a book using POST
- Fetched it using GET
- Opened the database
- Saw the BOOK table
- You saw that your Java object was actually stored inside a real database table.

Now the important question is:

**Which database were we using?** \
The Database We Used: **H2**

---

In our previous example, we were using a database called **H2**. \
H2 is:
- A lightweight, high-performance database management system written in Java
- Very easy to set up
- Runs inside your Spring Boot application
- Perfect for learning and testing

That’s why we used it for this demo.

---

Now, let’s properly configure H2 step-by-step:
1. Add `H2` dependency
2. Configure `application.properties`
3. Open H2 console

Next, Let’s start with adding the dependency.
