pages.title: H2 Database Setup
pages.content:
To use H2 database in our Spring Boot project, we must add its dependency. 

**Step 1: Adding H2 Dependency** \
If you are using Spring Initializr to download the dependency as you've learned earlier then, just select:
- Spring Data JPA
- H2 Database

If adding manually in `pom.xml`, add this:
```java


	org.springframework.boot
	spring-boot-starter-data-jpa




	com.h2database
	h2
	runtime

```

1. **`spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`** \
This dependency:
- Adds JPA support
- Adds Hibernate (ORM implementation)
- Enables repository features like:
```java
bookRepository.save(book);
bookRepository.findAll();
```
- You don’t write SQL manually.
- JPA + Hibernate handle database operations for you.

2. **`h2` Dependency** \
This dependency:
- Adds H2 database to our project
- Allows Spring Boot to connect to it
- Enables H2 console

Without this, database won’t work.

---

**Step 2: Configure `application.properties`** \
Now we tell Spring Boot how to connect to H2. \
Open:
```sss
src/main/resources/application.properties
```

Add this configuration:
```json
# H2 Database Config
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
spring.datasource.driverClassName=org.h2.Driver
spring.datasource.username=sa
spring.datasource.password=
spring.jpa.database-platform=org.hibernate.dialect.H2Dialect

# Show SQL in console
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# Automatically create tables
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=update

# Enable H2 Console
spring.h2.console.enabled=true
spring.h2.console.path=/h2-console
spring.h2.console.settings.web-allow-others=true
spring.h2.console.settings.trace=false
```

**What These Important Lines Mean**
```java
jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
```
- mem means in-memory database
- Data exists while app is running
- Restart → data gone

**`ddl-auto=update`** \
This tells Hibernate:
- Automatically create or update tables based on our `@Entity` classes.
- So when we create: 
```java
@Entity
public class Book { ... }
```
- Table is automatically created.
- No manual SQL needed.


**`show-sql=true`**
- This prints SQL queries in console.
- So when we call:
```java
bookRepository.save(book);
```
**You will see:**
```sss
insert into book ...
```
This helps students see ORM in action.

---

**Step 3: Open H2 Console** \
After running the application, open:

If port is 3000:
```java
http://localhost:3000/h2-console
```
Login with:
```sss
JDBC URL: jdbc:h2:mem:testdb
Username: sa
Password: (leave empty)
```
Click **Connect**.

Now you can see your tables.

---

**What Just Happened?** \
When the app starts:
- Spring Boot connects to `H2`
- Hibernate reads `@Entity`
- Table is created automatically
- Repository works with database
- All automatically.

That’s the power of **Spring Boot + JPA + H2**.

practiceProblems.title: Understanding Entity & Repository
practiceProblems.description:
Till now, we understood the flow: \
**Object → JPA → Hibernate → Database** \
We also saw how our Book object was stored inside a real database table.

---

**Before we begin...**
1. Run your Spring Boot app.
2. API Tester will open in the lab browser.
3. Add a book using POST.
4. Open H2 Console \
In the lab URL, after `codechef-apps.com` Add :
```sss
/h2-console/login.jsp
```
Login Page will get open : \
Enter: 
- JDBC URL : `jdbc:h2:mem:testdb`
- Username : `sa`
- Password : (leave empty)
- Click **Connect**.
5. Run Query `SELECT * FROM BOOK;`, You'll see `BOOK` table

---

Now it’s time to understand how we actually write the code that makes this happen. \
In this section, we will continue using our previous Book demo example.


---

**Step 1: Creating an Entity** \
Look at the code in IDE: \
We created a class - `Book.java` :
```java
import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class Book {

 @Id
 @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
 private Long id;

 private String title;
 private String author;

 // getters and setters
}
```

**`@Entity` :** \
`@Entity` tells JPA: \
"This class should be converted into a database table." \
So: **Book class → BOOK table**


**`@Id` :** \
`@Id` tells JPA: \
"This field is the Primary Key." \
Every table must have a primary key. \
Here: `private Long id;` - is the primary key.

**`@GeneratedValue` :**
```java
@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
```
This tells: \
"Database should automatically generate the ID." 

So when we save:
```java
new Book("Spring", "John");
```
We don’t manually set ID. \
Database creates it automatically.

---

**Step 2: Creating Repository** \
Now we need a way to talk to the database. \
Instead of writing SQL, we create an interface `BookRepository`:
```java
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;

public interface BookRepository extends JpaRepository {
}
```
That’s it.
No implementation. No SQL.

**What is `JpaRepository`?** 
- This means:
 - Book → Entity type
 - Long → Type of Primary Key (id)
- Spring automatically creates implementation at runtime.


**What Do We Get Automatically?**
Without writing any code, we get:
```sss
save(book);
findAll();
findById(id);
deleteById(id);
```
All CRUD operations are already available.

**Big Picture From Example**
`@Entity` → Creates table
`@Id` → Primary key
`@GeneratedValue` → Auto ID
`JpaRepository` → Ready-made CRUD

No SQL.
No implementation class.
Just annotations and interface.

---

**Step 3: Controller Using Repository** \
Now look at the code in IDE: \
Open `BookController.java`: \
This is the **Controller layer** that exposes APIs for the Book application.

The controller does **not talk to the database directly**.
Instead, it uses **`BookRepository`** to perform database operations.


**Repository Injection :** \
Inside the controller, you will see that BookRepository is injected using constructor injection. \
This means Spring automatically provides the repository object when the application starts. \
So the controller can directly use the repository to perform database operations.

**POST API — Save Book** \
When a client sends a request to:
```java
POST /api/books
```
The request body contains a **Book object**. \
The controller receives this object and calls the repository to **save it**.

**Behind the scenes:**
1. Controller receives the request.
2. Controller calls the repository.
3. Spring Data JPA passes the object to **Hibernate**.
4. Hibernate converts the object into **SQL INSERT**.
5. The book is stored in the **database table**.

**GET API — Fetch Books** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
GET /api/books
```
The controller simply **calls the repository to fetch all books**.

**Behind the scenes:**
1. Repository requests data from the database.
2. Hibernate runs a **SQL SELECT query**.
3. The rows from the table are converted into **Book objects**.
4. The controller returns them as a response.

---

**Complete Flow Now** \
From the moment a user sends a request:
```sss
Client Request → Controller → Repository → JPA → Hibernate → Database
```
And when data is returned:
```sss
Database → Hibernate → JPA → Repository → Controller → Response
```
This is how **Entity, Repository**, and **Controller** work together to store and retrieve data from the database.

practiceProblems.title: CRUD Operations with Spring Data JPA
practiceProblems.description:
In the previous section, we learned that Spring Data JPA automatically provides CRUD methods when we extend JpaRepository. \
Now let’s understand this through a simple demo example.

In this example, we built a Student Manager API using the same project structure you already know:
- **model** → `Student.java`
- **repository** → `StudentRepository.java`
- **controller** → `StudentController.java`

---

**Try It Yourself :** 

**1. Create Student (POST)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
POST /api/students
```
The controller receives the student data and calls the repository to **save the student**.

Behind the scenes:
```sss
Controller → Repository → Hibernate → Database
```
Hibernate generates an INSERT SQL query and stores the student in the database.

**To See Database :** \
Open H2 Console \
In the lab URL, after `codechef-apps.com` Add :
```sss
/h2-console/login.jsp
```
Login Page will get open : \
Enter: 
- JDBC URL : `jdbc:h2:mem:testdb`
- Username : `sa`
- Password : (leave empty)
- Click **Connect**.
5. Run Query `SELECT * FROM STUDENT;`, You'll see `STUDENT` table :


**2. Get All Students (GET)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
GET /api/students
```
The controller calls the repository to fetch all students. \
Hibernate runs a SELECT query, converts the rows into Student objects, and returns them.

**3. Get Student By ID (GET)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
GET /api/students/{id}
```
The repository fetches the student with that specific ID from the database.

**4. Update Student (PUT)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
PUT /api/students/{id}
```
The controller updates the student data and calls `save()` again. \
Hibernate automatically generates an UPDATE SQL query.

---

**Let's see how the code works step by step**

**Step 1: Entity (`Student.java`)**
- First, look at the file `Student.java` inside the model folder.
- This class represents the data structure of a student.
- Using the `@Entity` annotation, we tell JPA:
 “This class should be converted into a database table.”
- So the mapping becomes:

- The `@Id` annotation marks the primary key, and
- `@GeneratedValue` tells the database to generate the ID automatically.

So whenever we create a new student, the **database assigns the ID automatically**.

**Step 2: Repository (`StudentRepository.java`)** \
Next, open `StudentRepository.java` in the repository folder. \
Here we create a simple interface that extends JpaRepository. \
This is where Spring Data JPA becomes powerful. \
Just by extending JpaRepository, we automatically get several built-in CRUD methods such as:
- `save()` → Insert or update data
- `findAll()` → Get all records
- `findById()` → Get record by ID
- `deleteById()` → Delete record by ID

The important thing here is: \
We did not write any SQL queries or implementation code. \
Spring Boot automatically generates the implementation at runtime.


**Step 3: Controller (`StudentController.java`)** \
Now open `StudentController.java` in the controller folder. \
The controller exposes APIs that allow users to interact with the application.
Inside the controller, we use `StudentRepository` to perform database operations.

5. Run Query `SELECT * FROM STUDENT;`, You'll see `STUDENT` table :


**2. Get All Students (GET)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
GET /api/students
```
The controller calls the repository to fetch all students. \
Hibernate runs a SELECT query, converts the rows into Student objects, and returns them.

**3. Get Student By ID (GET)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
GET /api/students/{id}
```
The repository fetches the student with that specific ID from the database.

**4. Update Student (PUT)** \
When a request is sent to:
```java
PUT /api/students/{id}
```
The controller updates the student data and calls `save()` again. \
Hibernate automatically generates an UPDATE SQL query.

---

**Let's see how the code works step by step**

**Step 1: Entity (`Student.java`)**
- First, look at the file `Student.java` inside the model folder.
- This class represents the data structure of a student.
- Using the `@Entity` annotation, we tell JPA:
 “This class should be converted into a database table.”
- So the mapping becomes:

- The `@Id` annotation marks the primary key, and
- `@GeneratedValue` tells the database to generate the ID automatically.

So whenever we create a new student, the **database assigns the ID automatically**.

**Step 2: Repository (`StudentRepository.java`)** \
Next, open `StudentRepository.java` in the repository folder. \
Here we create a simple interface that extends JpaRepository. \
This is where Spring Data JPA becomes powerful. \
Just by extending JpaRepository, we automatically get several built-in CRUD methods such as:
- `save()` → Insert or update data
- `findAll()` → Get all records
- `findById()` → Get record by ID
- `deleteById()` → Delete record by ID

The important thing here is: \
We did not write any SQL queries or implementation code. \
Spring Boot automatically generates the implementation at runtime.


**Step 3: Controller (`StudentController.java`)** \
Now open `StudentController.java` in the controller folder. \
The controller exposes APIs that allow users to interact with the application.
Inside the controller, we use `StudentRepository` to perform database operations.

practiceProblems.title: Corporate Asset Registry Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Learners!** Welcome to the **Corporate Asset Registry Project!** 

In this project, you will build a **Spring Boot Backend** that acts as a digital ledger for a modern company. It allows the company to track, organize, and manage their physical assets like laptops and vehicles.

**Efficient management is key!** Chef needs a reliable system to know exactly what equipment they own, how much it cost, and who is currently using it. Your system will use **Spring Data JPA** to talk to a database automatically without writing raw SQL.

Your **task** is to **complete the missing backend logic** to make this API fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **4 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
1. `Asset.java` → **Entity:** (The Data Model) that maps a Java class to a Database Table.
2. `AssetRepository.java` → **Repository** (The Data Access Layer) that handles saving and retrieving data.
3. `AssetService.java` → **Service** (The Business Logic) that controls the flow of data.
4. `AssetController.java` → **Controller** (The API Layer) that handles web requests from the frontend.

**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: CRUD & JPA** \
This project uses the **CRUD** pattern (Create, Read, Update, Delete). Instead of writing complex SQL queries, we use **Spring Data JPA**.
1. **Entity:** You define a Java class, and Spring creates the table for you.
2. **Repository:** You extend an interface, and Spring generates the code to `save()`, `delete()`, or `findAll()`.
3. **Derived Queries:** You can even invent new searches just by naming methods correctly, like `findByBirthDate()` or `findByCategory()`.

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:
1. Run the file named `consoleViewer.js` and paste the CodeChef browser URL. For more details, refer to the project demonstration video.
 - Command to run the file:
 ```default
 node consoleViewer.js
 ```
2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:assetdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Entity** \
 **File:** `entity/Asset.java` This class represents a single item in our database.
 - **Annotations:** Mark the class as a JPA entity and map it to a table named `"corporate_assets"`.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field to be the Primary Key and set it to **Auto-Increment** using the `IDENTITY` strategy.
 - **Constructors:** Implement the **Default Constructor** (required by JPA) and the **Parameterized Constructor** to initialize fields.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data. \
**Docs:** Anatomy of a Java Class | Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue

2. **Configure the Repository** \
 **File:** `repository/AssetRepository.java` This interface is your direct line to the database.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Repository.
 - **Inheritance:** Make this interface extend `JpaRepository`. You must specify the **Entity type** (`Asset`) and the **ID type** (`Long`).
 - **Derived Query:** Write a method signature that tells Spring to select assets based on their `category`.
 - *Hint:* The method name must start with `findBy...`. \
**Docs:** @Repository Annotation | Spring Data Derived Queries | JpaRepository Interface

3. **Build the Service (The Brain)** \
 **File:** `service/AssetService.java` This is where the logic lives. It sits between the Controller and the Repository.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define a `final` variable for the Repository and initialize it using a Constructor.
 - **Implement Methods:**
 - Implement the logic for adding and viewing assets by directly calling the repository's built-in `save()`, `findAll()`, and `findById()` methods.
 - Implement the category search by calling the custom method you defined in the Repository.
 - **Update:** First, find the asset by ID. If it exists, update its fields and save it again. If not, return `null`.
 - **Delete:** Check if the asset exists. If yes, delete it and return a success message. If not, return a **Not Found** message. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data save() Method

4. **Define the API Endpoints (The Controller)** \
 **File:** `controller/AssetController.java` This class listens for web requests (JSON) from the frontend.
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Initialize the `AssetService` using the constructor.
 - **Map the Endpoints:**
 - **Add Asset** (`/add`): Create an endpoint to handle creation requests. You need to map the incoming JSON body to your `Asset` object.
 - **Get All** (`/all`): Create an endpoint that retrieves and returns the complete list of assets.
 - **Get by ID** (`/{id}`): Create an endpoint to find a single asset. You must **extract the dynamic ID** directly from the URL path.
 - **Get by Category** (`/category/{category}`): Create an endpoint to filter assets. Like the ID, you need to **extract the category name** from the URL.
 - **Update Asset** (`/update/{id}`): Create an endpoint to modify an asset. This method requires capturing **two** pieces of data: the ID from the URL and the updated asset details from the request body.
 - **Delete Asset** (`/delete/{id}`): Create an endpoint to remove an asset. Capture the ID from the URL to tell the service which item to delete. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | @GetMapping & @PostMapping | Spring @PathVariable | @RequestBody Annotation

---

**Expected Behaviour:** \
Before submitting the project, ensure the **backend server is running**. If you make any changes to the code, you must **restart the server** for those changes to take effect.

constraints:
- $1 \leq T \leq 100$
- $1 \leq N \leq 100$
- $1 \leq M \leq N\cdot(N-1)/2$
- $1 \leq u_i, v_i \leq N$
- $u_i \neq v_i$ for each $1 \leq i \leq M$.
- The sum of $N$ over all test cases won't exceed $100$.
practiceProblems.inputFormat:
- The first line of input will contain a single integer $T$, denoting the number of test cases.
- Each test case consists of multiple lines of input.
 - The first line of each test case contains two space-separated integers $N$ and $M$ — the number of vertices and edges of the graph, respectively.
 - The next $M$ lines describe the edges. The $i$-th of these $M$ lines contains two space-separated integers $u_i$ and $v_i$, denoting an edge between $u_i$ and $v_i$.
practiceProblems.outputFormat: For each test case, output on a new line the number of good subgraphs of $G$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

practiceProblems.title: IoT Nexus Controller Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Innovators!** Welcome to the **IoT Nexus Controller Project!** 

In this project, you will build the **Spring Boot Backend** for a next-generation Smart Home Hub. This system acts as the central "brain" that organizes and controls smart devices across different locations in a house.

**Connectivity is everything!** A modern smart home needs to know which devices (like Smart Bulbs, Thermostats, or Cameras) belong to which specific room (like the Living Room or Kitchen). Your system will use **Spring Data JPA Relationships** to link these items together automatically.

Your **task** is to **complete the missing backend logic** to make this API fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **6 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
 - **Entities (The Data Model):**
 - `Room.java` → The **Parent** entity. Represents a physical location (e.g., "Kitchen").
 - `Device.java` → The **Child** entity. Represents a gadget (e.g., "Smart Bulb") that belongs to a Room.
 - **Repositories (The Data Access Layer):**
 - `RoomRepository.java` & `DeviceRepository.java` → Interfaces that handle saving and retrieving data for their respective entities.
 - **Service (The Business Logic):**
 - `IoTService.java` → Contains the logic to **link** devices to rooms and handle cascading deletions.
 - **Controller (The API Layer):**
 - `IoTController.java` → Handles web requests to create rooms, add devices, and manage the system.


**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: ORM Relationships** \
This project focuses on **Object-Relational Mapping (ORM)**. We are not just storing simple lists; we are storing **Relationships**.
1. **One-to-Many:** One Room can have Many Devices.
2. **Many-to-One:** Many Devices belong to One Room.
3. **Cascading:** If you delete a Room, the system should automatically delete all Devices inside it (because a wall switch cannot exist without a wall!).

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:
1. Run the file named `consoleViewer.js` and paste the CodeChef browser URL. For more details, refer to the project demonstration video.
 - Command to run the file:
 ```default
 node consoleViewer.js
 ```
2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:iotdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Entities**
- **File:** `entity/Room.java` (The Parent)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field to be the Primary Key and set it to **Auto-Increment** using the `IDENTITY` strategy.
 - **Relationship:** Define a list of devices using One To Many Mapping.
 - **Challenge 1:** Configure this relationship so that Hibernate knows the Device class is the "owner" of the link (*Hint:* Explore the `mappedby` attribute). 
 - **Challenge 2:** Configure the cascading behaviour so that if a Room is Deleted or Saved, that action automatically applies to all its Devices as well.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data.
- **File:** `entity/Device.java` (The Child)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field as the Primary Key with Auto-Increment.
 - **The Relationship (Link to Room):**
 - Define a relationship where **many** Devices can belong to **one** Room.
 - **Foreign Key Challenge:** Configure the joining column name in the database table to be `"room_id"`.
 - **JSON Challenge:** Add a specific annotation to this field to prevent an **"Infinite Recursion"** loop (Room → Device → Room...) when the data is converted to JSON.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields. \
**Docs:** Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue | Guide to @OneToMany and @ManyToOne | 
Understanding the mappedBy Attribute | JPA Cascade Types | Using @JoinColumn for Foreign Keys | Handling Infinite Recursion with @JsonIgnore

2. **Configure the Repositories** \
 **File:** `repository/RoomRepository.java` & `repository/DeviceRepository.java` These interfaces are your direct line to the database.
 - **Interface:** Define these as Interfaces (not classes).
 - **Inheritance:** Extend the standard `JpaRepository` interface.
 - **Generics:** You must specify two things for each repository:
 1. The **Entity Type** it manages (`Room` or `Device`).
 2. The **Data Type** of that Entity's Primary Key. \
**Docs:** @Repository Annotation | Introduction to Spring Data JPA Repositories | JpaRepository Interface | Java Generics (The syntax)

3. **Build the Service** \
 **File:** `service/IoTService.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define the repositories as `private final` fields and initialize them using a **Constructor**.
 - **Logic - Add Device:**
 - Try to find the `Room` using its ID.
 - If the Room exists, **LINK** the device to the room (set the relationship).
 - Save the device to the database.
 - If the Room does not exist, throw an exception (code provided).
 - **Logic - Delete Room:**
 - Delete the Room by its ID. Because of the **Cascading** you configured in step 1, this should automatically remove all associated devices.
 - **Logic - Delete Device:**
 - Check if the device exists, then delete it. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data CrudRepository Methods (save, findById)

4. **Define the API Endpoints** \
 **File:** `controller/IoTController.java`
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Inject the `IoTService` using the constructor.
 - **Map the Endpoints:**
 1. **Create a Room** (`/rooms`)
 - **Goal:** Save a new room to the database.
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle POST requests.
 - **Input:** The room data is coming as JSON. Use the correct annotation to convert that JSON body into a `Room` Java object.
 2. **Get All Rooms** (`/rooms`)
 - **Goal:** Retrieve the list of all rooms (and their devices).
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle GET requests.
 - **Output:** Return a `List`.
 3. **Add Device** (`/rooms/{roomId}/devices`)
 - **Goal:** Add a new device to a specific room.
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle POST requests.
 - **Inputs:** You need to capture two pieces of data from different places:
 - Extract Room ID from the URL Path (the {roomId} part).
 - Extract Device Data from the Request Body (the JSON sent by the user).
 4. **Delete Room** (`/rooms/{id}`)
 - **Goal:** Remove a room (and automatically remove its devices).
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle DELETE requests.
 - **Input:** Extract the id from the URL Path so the service knows which room to delete.
 5. **Delete Device** (`/devices/{id}`)
 - **Goal:** Remove a single device. 
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle DELETE requests.
 - **Input:** Extract the id from the URL Path. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | Overview of @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @DeleteMapping | Spring @PathVariable | @RequestBody Annotation

---

**Expected Behaviour:** \
Before submitting the project, ensure the **backend server is running**. If you make any changes to the code, you must **restart the server** for those changes to take effect.

You are given **6 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
 - **Entities (The Data Model):**
 - `Room.java` → The **Parent** entity. Represents a physical location (e.g., "Kitchen").
 - `Device.java` → The **Child** entity. Represents a gadget (e.g., "Smart Bulb") that belongs to a Room.
 - **Repositories (The Data Access Layer):**
 - `RoomRepository.java` & `DeviceRepository.java` → Interfaces that handle saving and retrieving data for their respective entities.
 - **Service (The Business Logic):**
 - `IoTService.java` → Contains the logic to **link** devices to rooms and handle cascading deletions.
 - **Controller (The API Layer):**
 - `IoTController.java` → Handles web requests to create rooms, add devices, and manage the system.


**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: ORM Relationships** \
This project focuses on **Object-Relational Mapping (ORM)**. We are not just storing simple lists; we are storing **Relationships**.
1. **One-to-Many:** One Room can have Many Devices.
2. **Many-to-One:** Many Devices belong to One Room.
3. **Cascading:** If you delete a Room, the system should automatically delete all Devices inside it (because a wall switch cannot exist without a wall!).

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:
1. Run the file named `consoleViewer.js` and paste the CodeChef browser URL. For more details, refer to the project demonstration video.
 - Command to run the file:
 ```default
 node consoleViewer.js
 ```
2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:iotdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Entities**
- **File:** `entity/Room.java` (The Parent)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field to be the Primary Key and set it to **Auto-Increment** using the `IDENTITY` strategy.
 - **Relationship:** Define a list of devices using One To Many Mapping.
 - **Challenge 1:** Configure this relationship so that Hibernate knows the Device class is the "owner" of the link (*Hint:* Explore the `mappedby` attribute). 
 - **Challenge 2:** Configure the cascading behaviour so that if a Room is Deleted or Saved, that action automatically applies to all its Devices as well.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data.
- **File:** `entity/Device.java` (The Child)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field as the Primary Key with Auto-Increment.
 - **The Relationship (Link to Room):**
 - Define a relationship where **many** Devices can belong to **one** Room.
 - **Foreign Key Challenge:** Configure the joining column name in the database table to be `"room_id"`.
 - **JSON Challenge:** Add a specific annotation to this field to prevent an **"Infinite Recursion"** loop (Room → Device → Room...) when the data is converted to JSON.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields. \
**Docs:** Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue | Guide to @OneToMany and @ManyToOne | 
Understanding the mappedBy Attribute | JPA Cascade Types | Using @JoinColumn for Foreign Keys | Handling Infinite Recursion with @JsonIgnore

2. **Configure the Repositories** \
 **File:** `repository/RoomRepository.java` & `repository/DeviceRepository.java` These interfaces are your direct line to the database.
 - **Interface:** Define these as Interfaces (not classes).
 - **Inheritance:** Extend the standard `JpaRepository` interface.
 - **Generics:** You must specify two things for each repository:
 1. The **Entity Type** it manages (`Room` or `Device`).
 2. The **Data Type** of that Entity's Primary Key. \
**Docs:** @Repository Annotation | Introduction to Spring Data JPA Repositories | JpaRepository Interface | Java Generics (The syntax)

3. **Build the Service** \
 **File:** `service/IoTService.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define the repositories as `private final` fields and initialize them using a **Constructor**.
 - **Logic - Add Device:**
 - Try to find the `Room` using its ID.
 - If the Room exists, **LINK** the device to the room (set the relationship).
 - Save the device to the database.
 - If the Room does not exist, throw an exception (code provided).
 - **Logic - Delete Room:**
 - Delete the Room by its ID. Because of the **Cascading** you configured in step 1, this should automatically remove all associated devices.
 - **Logic - Delete Device:**
 - Check if the device exists, then delete it. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data CrudRepository Methods (save, findById)

4. **Define the API Endpoints** \
 **File:** `controller/IoTController.java`
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Inject the `IoTService` using the constructor.
 - **Map the Endpoints:**
 1. **Create a Room** (`/rooms`)
 - **Goal:** Save a new room to the database.
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle POST requests.

 - **Goal:** Retrieve the list of all rooms (and their devices).
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle GET requests.
 - **Output:** Return a `List`.
 3. **Add Device** (`/rooms/{roomId}/devices`)
 - **Goal:** Add a new device to a specific room.
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle POST requests.
 - **Inputs:** You need to capture two pieces of data from different places:
 - Extract Room ID from the URL Path (the {roomId} part).
 - Extract Device Data from the Request Body (the JSON sent by the user).
 4. **Delete Room** (`/rooms/{id}`)
 - **Goal:** Remove a room (and automatically remove its devices).
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle DELETE requests.
 - **Input:** Extract the id from the URL Path so the service knows which room to delete.
 5. **Delete Device** (`/devices/{id}`)
 - **Goal:** Remove a single device. 
 - **Action:** Map this method to handle DELETE requests.
 - **Input:** Extract the id from the URL Path. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | Overview of @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @DeleteMapping | Spring @PathVariable | @RequestBody Annotation

practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Coders!** Welcome to the **Tech Blog Platform Project** 

In this project, you will build the **Spring Boot Backend** for a content publishing engine. This system acts as the backbone for a blogging site where creators can publish articles and readers can engage with them.

A blog isn't just a list of words; it's a web of relationships. **Authors** write **Posts**, and **Posts** generate **Comments**. Your system will use JPA Mappings to chain these entities together seamlessly.

Your **task** is to **complete the missing backend logic** to make this API fully functional.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **8 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
 - **Entities (The Data Model):**
 - `Author.java` → The **Root** entity. Represents the content creator.
 - `BlogPost.java` → The **Middle** entity. Represents an article written by an Author.
 - `Comment.java` → The **Leaf** entity. Represents reader feedback on a specific Post.
 - **Repositories (The Data Access Layer):**
 - `AuthorRepository`, `BlogPostRepository` & `CommentRepository` → Interfaces that handle saving and retrieving data for their respective entities.
 - **Service (The Business Logic):**
 - `BlogService.java` → Contains the logic to **link** posts to authors, comments to posts, and handle cascading deletions.
 - **Controller (The API Layer):**
 - `BlogController.java` → Handles web requests to publish posts, add comments, and fetch the feed.

**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: ORM Relationships** \
This project focuses on **Chained Relationships** and **Performance Tuning**.
1. **The Hierarchy:** Author BlogPost Comment.
2. **Cascading:**
 - If you delete an **Author**, the system must delete all their **Posts**.
 - If you delete a **Post**, the system must delete all its **Comments**.
3. **Fetch Types (Performance):**
 - **LAZY:** When loading an Author, don't load their 500 posts immediately (Too heavy!).
 - **EAGER:** When loading a Comment, do load the Post info immediately (We need context!).

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:
1. Run the file named `consoleViewer.js` and paste the CodeChef browser URL. For more details, refer to the project demonstration video.
 - Command to run the file:
 ```default
 node consoleViewer.js
 ```
2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:techblogdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Entities**
- **File:** `entity/Author.java` (The Root)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class as a JPA Entity.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field to be the Primary Key and set it to **Auto-Increment** using the `IDENTITY` strategy.
 - **Relationship:** Define a list of `blogPosts` using **One-to-Many**.
 - **Challenge 1:** Map it to the `author` field in the `BlogPost` class.
 - **Challenge 2:** Configure `cascade` to **ALL** (Delete Author Delete Posts).
 - **Challenge 2:** Set `fetch` to **LAZY** (Performance optimization).
 - **JSON Handling:** Add the annotation to **ignore** this list during JSON conversion (Stop Infinite Loops).
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data.
- **File:** `entity/BlogPost.java` (The Connector)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field as the Primary Key with Auto-Increment.
 - **Content Field:** The default storage is too small (255 chars).
 - **Challenge:** Add an annotation to set the column length to `5000` characters.
 - **Relationship 1 (Link to Author):**
 - Many Posts belong to One Author.
 - **Fetch:** Set to **EAGER** (Load author name with post).
 - **Foreign Key:** Name the column `"author_id"`.
 - **Relationship 2 (Link to Comments):**
 - One Post has Many Comments.
 - **MappedBy:** Point to the `blogPost` field in Comment.
 - **Cascade:** Set to **REMOVE** (Delete Post Delete Comments).
 - **Fetch:** Set to **LAZY**.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data.
- **File:** `entity/Comment.java` (The Leaf)
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field as the Primary Key with Auto-Increment.
 - **Relationship (Link to Post):**
 - Many Comments belong to One Post.
 - **Fetch:** Set to **EAGER**.
 - **Foreign Key:** Name the column `"blogpost_id"`.
 - **JSON Handling:** Add annotation to **ignore** the `blogPost` field (Stop Infinite Loops).
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data. \
**Docs:** Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue | Guide to @OneToMany and @ManyToOne | 
Understanding the mappedBy Attribute | JPA Cascade Types | Using @JoinColumn for Foreign Keys | Handling Infinite Recursion with @JsonIgnore

2. **Configure the Repositories** (Code Provided) \
 **File:** `AuthorRepository`, `BlogPostRepository`, `CommentRepository`
 - **Interface:** Define these as Interfaces (not classes).
 - **Inheritance:** Extend the standard `JpaRepository` interface.
 - **Generics:** Specify the Entity Type (e.g., `Author`) and ID Type (e.g., `Long`).

3. **Build the Service** \
 **File:** `service/BlogService.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define the 3 repositories as `private final` fields and initialize them via **Constructor Injection**.
 - **Logic - Create Post:**
 - Find the `Author` by ID (use `.orElse(null)` logic).
 - If found, **LINK** the Post to the Author (Foreign Key).
 - Save the Post.
 - If not found, throw RuntimeException.
 - **Logic - Add Comment:**
 - Find the `BlogPost` by ID.
 - If found, **LINK** the Comment to the Post.
 - Save the Comment.
 - **Logic - Delete Post:**
 - Delete by ID (Cascade settings in Entity will handle the rest).
 - **Logic - Get All Posts:**
 - Return the full list using the repository. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data CrudRepository Methods (save, findById)

4. **Define the API Endpoints** \
 **File:** `controller/BlogController.java`
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Inject the `BlogService` using the constructor.
 - **Endpoints:**
 1. **Create Author** (`POST /authors`)
 - Convert the JSON body to an Author object.
 - **Action:** Call the service method to save the author and return the saved object.
 2. **Create Post** (`POST /authors/{authorId}/posts`)
 - Capture `authorId` from the URL path.
 - Capture `post` data from the Request Body.
 - **Action:** Call the service method that links the post to the author.
 3. **Add Comment** (`POST /posts/{postId}/comments`)
 - Capture `postId` from the URL path.
 - Capture `comment` data from the Request Body.
 - **Action:** Call the service method to add the comment.
 4. **Get Feed** (`GET /posts`)
 - **Action:** Call the service method to get all posts and return the list.
 5. **Delete Post** (`DELETE /posts/{postId}`)
 - Capture `postId` from the URL path.
 - **Action:** Call the service to delete the post (and its comments via Cascade). \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | Building a RESTful Web Service | Overview of @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @DeleteMapping | Spring @PathVariable | @RequestBody Annotation

---

**Expected Behaviour:** \
Before submitting the project, ensure the **backend server is running**. If you make any changes to the code, you must **restart the server** for those changes to take effect.

practiceProblems.title: Flight Booking Engine Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hello Developers!** Welcome to the **Flight Booking Engine Project** 

In this project, you will build a **Spring Boot Backend** for an airline reservation system. \
A booking system isn't just about saving data, it's about **Integrity**. When a user books a ticket, two things must happen:
1. The seat count must decrease.
2. The payment must be processed.

What happens if the seat is taken, but the payment fails immediately after? Does the airline lose a seat for free? \
Your task is to implement **Transaction Management** to ensure that these two steps happen together (Commit) or not at all (Rollback).

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **6 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
 - **Entities (The Data Model):**
 - `Flight.java` → Represents the aircraft and available inventory (seats).
 - `PaymentInfo.java` → Represents the financial transaction details.
 - **Repositories (The Data Access Layer):**
 - `FlightRepository` & `PaymentRepository` → Interfaces that handle database operations.
 - **Service (The Business Logic):**
 - `BookingService.java` → Contains the **logic** to deduct seats and validate payments atomically.
 - **Controller (The API Layer):**
 - `FlightController.java` → Handles web requests to check seat status and book tickets.

**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: Transactions & Rollback** \
This project focuses on **Atomicity**.
- **Rule:** A Flight Booking is considered "Complete" only if **BOTH** the seat is deducted AND the payment is saved.
- **Fail Scenario:** If a user tries to pay more than **$500** (Backend Limit), the system throws an exception.
- **Requirement:** If the exception occurs, the system must **Undo (Rollback)** the seat deduction automatically.

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:

2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:flightdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

**Pre-Loaded Data (`data.sql`)** \
To help you test immediately, we have pre-loaded the database with one flight using the `resources/data.sql` file:
- Flight ID: `1`, Flight Number: `CC-101`, Destination: `Bengaluru`, Available Seats: `10`.

1. **Complete the Entities**

 - **Constructors:** Implement the All-Args constructor.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data.
- **File:** `entity/PaymentInfo.java`
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class so that JPA recognizes it as a database table.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field as the Primary Key with Auto-Increment.
 - **Constructors:** Implement the All-Args constructor.
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data. \
**Docs:** Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue

2. **Configure the Repositories** \
 **File:** `repository/FlightRepository.java` & `repository/PaymentRepository.java` These interfaces are your direct line to the database.
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark these interfaces as a Repository.
 - **Inheritance:** Extend the standard `JpaRepository` interface.
 - **Generics:** You must specify two things for each repository:
 1. The **Entity Type** it manages (e.g., `Flight`).
 2. The **Data Type** of that Entity's Primary Key. \
**Docs:** @Repository Annotation | Introduction to Spring Data JPA Repositories | JpaRepository Interface | Java Generics (The syntax)

3. **Build the Service** \
 **File:** `service/BookingService.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define the 2 repositories as `private final` fields and initialize them via **Constructor Injection**.
 - **Transaction:** Apply the correct annotation to the `bookFlight` method to enable Atomic behaviour.
 - **Logic Flow:**
 - Use the `flightId` from the payment info to look up the flight. If the flight does not exist in the database, the process must stop immediately with an error.
 - Verify that the flight actually has seats available. You cannot book a seat on a full flight.
 - If valid, decrease the flight's `availableSeats` count by 1 and update the database.
 - Apply the business rule: **Any payment amount greater than 500 is invalid**. If this condition is met, throw a `RuntimeException`. This exception is the trigger that tests if your Rollback logic is working.
 - If the payment is within limits, save the `PaymentInfo` to the database. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Understanding @Transactional | Rolling Back Transactions | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data CrudRepository Methods (save, findById) | Java Optional Class

 **File:** `controller/FlightController.java`
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Inject the `BookingService` using the constructor.
 - **Endpoint 1: Get Flight** (`GET /api/{id}`)
 - Retrieve the flight details using the provided ID.
 - Return the `Flight` object if found, otherwise return an error.
 - **Endpoint 2: Book Flight** (`POST /api/book`)
 - Receive the `PaymentInfo` JSON and pass it to the service.
 - If the service completes successfully, return a standard **200 OK** response.
 - If the transaction fails (due to the Payment Limit exception), you must catch that failure and return a **500 Internal Server** Error to the client. \

Before submitting the project, ensure the **backend server is running**. If you make any changes to the code, you must **restart the server** for those changes to take effect.

1. The seat count must decrease.
2. The payment must be processed.

Your task is to implement **Transaction Management** to ensure that these two steps happen together (Commit) or not at all (Rollback).

---

 - **Service (The Business Logic):**

modules.description:
This module focuses on improving your Spring Boot APIs to make them ready for real-world use. You will learn how to handle errors using custom exceptions, ResponseEntity, and proper HTTP status codes.
It also covers input validation using annotations like @Valid, @NotNull, @Size, and @Email to ensure correct data. Additionally, you will learn to write custom queries using finder methods.
The module includes practice projects and explains the flow of handling requests, validating data, processing logic, and returning proper responses.

pages.title: Making APIs Production-Ready
pages.content:
Till now in the course, you have learned how to:
- Build REST APIs
- Use Spring Data JPA
- Store data in a database
- Perform CRUD operations

Your APIs are now **working correctly**.

---

But in real-world applications, **working is not enough**.
APIs must also be **reliable, safe**, and **user-friendly**.

For example, think about these situations:
- A user requests a product that does not exist
- A client sends invalid input data
- A database operation fails
- An API needs search and filtering

If we don't handle these cases properly, the API may return confusing errors or crash. \
So in this module, we will learn how to make our APIs production-ready.

---

Click on **"Next"**, To see various ways to make our APIs production-ready :

pages.title: Exception Handling
pages.content:
Before we learn how to handle exceptions in Spring Boot, let’s first understand what an exception actually is. \
An exception is an error that happens while the program is running. \
It usually occurs when something unexpected happens in the application.

---

**Imagine this request:**
```java
GET /api/products/10
```
But product **ID 10 does not exist** in the database.

**What should the API do?**
- Should it crash?
- Should it return null?
- Or should it return a proper error message?

In real APIs, we should return a **clear error response**. \
This is an **exception scenario**.

---

**Example:**
```sss
404 Not Found
Product with ID 10 not found
```
Handling these situations properly is called: \
**Exception Handling**

---

In the next section, we will start with - **Creating a Custom Exception**.

pages.title: Creating a Custom Exception
pages.content:
Now let’s handle the problem we discussed earlier. \
Imagine a user calls:

```jsx
GET /api/products/5
```

But product with ID `5` does not exist. \
Instead of returning null or a confusing error, we want to clearly say:
```sss
Product not found
```
To do this properly, **we create a custom exception**.

---

**What is a Custom Exception?** \
A custom exception is a **user-defined error** that we create for our application. \
It helps us clearly describe what went wrong.

**For example:**
- Product not found
- User not found
- Order not found

Instead of generic errors, we create **specific exceptions**.

Click on **"Next**, To see how to create specific exceptions.

pages.title: ResponseEntity in Spring Boot
pages.content:
`ResponseEntity` is a class in Spring Boot used to send a **complete HTTP response**. \
It allows us to control:
- Response Body (data)
- Status Code (200, 201, 404, etc.)
- Headers (optional)

---

**Why do we use it?** \
In real APIs, we don’t just send data — we also send **status information**. \
Example:
- Data found → **200 OK**
- Data created → **201 CREATED**
- Data not found → **404 NOT FOUND**

`ResponseEntity` helps us send both **data + status together**

---

**Syntax :**
```java
ResponseEntity
```
`T` = type of data you want to return

---

**Common Methods**
- **200 OK**
```java
ResponseEntity.ok(data);
```
- **201 Created**
```java
ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(data);
```
- **404 Not Found**
```java
ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
```

---

Now that you understand the concept, next let’s see this in action with a simple demo example, where we use `ResponseEntity` in a Spring Boot controller and test it.

pages.title: HTTP Status Codes
pages.content:
You have already used HTTP status codes while working with ResponseEntity. Now, let’s understand them more clearly and see what they represent in API responses.

HTTP status codes are **numeric codes** sent by the server in a response to indicate the **result of a request**. \
They help the client (browser/Postman/frontend) understand:
- whether the request was successful
- or if something went wrong

---

**Format** \
Every HTTP response contains a status code:
```sss
Status Code + Meaning
```
Example:
```sss
200 OK
404 NOT FOUND
```

---

**Why Status Codes are Important**
- Indicate success or failure of API calls
- Help frontend handle responses correctly
- Make APIs standard and predictable

---


**Categories of Status Codes** \
Status codes are grouped into 5 categories:

**1xx – Informational** \
Request received, processing continues \
Rarely used in APIs

**2xx – Success** \
Indicates the request was successful. \
Common codes:
- 200 OK → Request successful
- 201 CREATED → Resource created successfully

**3xx – Redirection**
- Request needs further action
- Used in URL redirection

Example:
```sss
302 Found
```

**4xx – Client Error** \
Indicates an error from the client side. \
Common codes:
- 400 BAD REQUEST → Invalid input
- 401 UNAUTHORIZED → Authentication required

404 NOT FOUND → Resource not found

**5xx – Server Error** \
Indicates server-side failure.
Common codes:
- 500 INTERNAL SERVER ERROR → Server crashed or failed
- 503 SERVICE UNAVAILABLE → Server not available


---

**Key Point**
- HTTP status codes describe the result of a request
- They are grouped into:
 - 1xx → Informational
 - 2xx → Success
 - 3xx → Redirection
 - 4xx → Client Error
 - 5xx → Server Error
- They are used with `ResponseEntity` to send proper API responses

practiceProblems.title: Demo - Custom Exception in Product API
practiceProblems.description:
**Understanding Custom Exception from the Code** \
Let’s first look at the code in the IDE and understand how the exception is created and used.

**We will follow a simple flow:**
1. Created a **custom exception class**. . 
2. Used that exception in the **ProductController**
3. See what happens when a product **exists vs does not exist**

**Step 1: Created the Exception Class** \
Firstly, created a new package:
```sss
exception
```
Inside this package, create the file:
```jsx
ProductNotFoundException.java
```
Code
```java
package com.example.demo.exception;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ResponseStatus;

@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND)
public class ProductNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {

 public ProductNotFoundException(String message) {
 super(message);
 }

}
```

**What this code does** \
Here we are creating **our own exception**.
- `ProductNotFoundException` is a **custom exception**
- It extends **`RuntimeException`**
- We pass a **custom error message**

Example message:
```sss
Product not found with id: 5
```
So whenever a product is missing, our application can **throw this exception with a clear message**.


**Step 2: Use the Exception in the Controller** \
Now open the controller:
```sss
ProductController.java
```
We will modify the **Get Product By ID API**.

Code
```java
package com.example.demo.controller;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.*;

import com.example.demo.model.Product;
import com.example.demo.repository.ProductRepository;
import com.example.demo.exception.ProductNotFoundException;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
public class ProductController {

 private final ProductRepository productRepository;

 public ProductController(ProductRepository productRepository) {
 this.productRepository = productRepository;
 }

 // Get product by ID
 @GetMapping("/{id}")
 public Product getProduct(@PathVariable Long id) {

 return productRepository.findById(id)
 .orElseThrow(() ->
 new ProductNotFoundException("Product not found with id: " + id)
 );
 }

}
```

**What Happens in This Code?** \
The important line is:
```java
productRepository.findById(id)
```
This method tries to **find a product in the database**. \
But this method does **not always return a product**. \
Instead, it returns:
```sss
Optional
```
This means the product **may exist or may not exist**.

---

**Case 1: Product Exists** \
Example request:
```json
GET /api/products/1
```
If product **ID 1 exists**, the API returns:
```json
{
 "id": 1,
 "name": "Laptop",
 "price": 50000
}
```
Everything works normally.

---

**Case 2: Product Does NOT Exist** \
Example request:
```java
GET /api/products/5
```
Suppose product ID `5` is not in the database. \
Then this code runs:
```java
.orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(...))
```
This tells Spring: \
If the product is not found, throw a `ProductNotFoundException`. 

So Spring throws:
```java
ProductNotFoundException
```
With message: 
```sss
Product not found with id: 5
```

---

**Flow of Execution**
```sss
Client Request
 ↓
GET /api/products/5
 ↓
Controller calls repository.findById()
 ↓
Product not found
 ↓
Throw ProductNotFoundException
```

practiceProblems.title: Demo Example (Book API using ResponseEntity)
practiceProblems.description:
Let’s go through the code and understand `ResponseEntity` from the Code: \
**1. Return Type**
```java
public ResponseEntity addBook(...)
```
- `ResponseEntity` → response contains a Book object
- Along with a status code

So each method returns: **status + data**

---

**2. CREATE API**
```java
return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(savedBook);
```
**What happens here:**
- status(HttpStatus.CREATED)` → sets HTTP status to 201
- `body(savedBook)` → sends the created book as response

**Final Response:**
- Status → 201 CREATED
- Body → saved book

---

**3. GET ALL API**
```java
return ResponseEntity.ok(service.getAllBooks());
```
**What happens here:**
- `ok()` → sets status to 200
- passes list of books as body

**Final Response:**
- Status → 200 OK
- Body → list of books

---

**4. GET BY ID API** \
**Step 1: Fetch book**
```java
Book book = service.getBookById(id);
```

**Case 1: Book not found**
```java
if (book == null) {
 return ResponseEntity.notFound().build();
}
```
- `notFound()` → sets status 404
- `build()` → no response body

**Final Response:** 
- Status → 404 NOT FOUND
- Body → empty


**Case 2: Book found**
```java
return ResponseEntity.ok(book);
```
- `ok()` → 200
- sends book as response

**Final Response:**
- Status → 200 OK
- Body → book

---

**Key Observation from This Code** \
Different methods return different status codes:
- **201** → when a book is created
- **200** → when data is successfully returned
- **404** → when data is not found

This control over the response is handled by `ResponseEntity`.

---

**Key Points :** \
From this example: 
1. `ResponseEntity` is used to return both:
- HTTP status code
- response data

2.Each API decides its response using:
- `status(...)`
- `ok(...)`
- `notFound()`

---

So, instead of returning only objects, the controller returns a **structured HTTP response** using `ResponseEntity`.

topics.title: Input Validation
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Input Validation.

pages.title: Input Validation in Spring Boot
pages.content:
Input validation is used to ensure that the data sent by the client is **correct and follows defined rules** before processing.

**For example:**
- Required fields should not be empty
- Text should have a minimum/maximum length
- Email should be in correct format

**Why Validation is Needed**
- Prevents invalid or incomplete data
- Improves API reliability
- Avoids errors during processing

---

**Validation Annotations** \
Spring Boot provides **built-in annotations for validation**:

**1. `@Valid`** \
Used in controller to trigger validation
```java
@PostMapping("/user")
public ResponseEntity addUser(@Valid @RequestBody User user)
```

**2. `@NotNull`** \
Field must not be null
```java
@NotNull
private String name;
```

**3. `@Size`** \
Defines minimum and maximum length
```java
@Size(min = 3, max = 10)
private String name;
```

**4. `@Email`** \
Validates email format
```java
@Email
private String email;
```

Click on **"NEXT"**, to understand this properly through an simple example

practiceProblems.title: Demo - Input validations in action
practiceProblems.description:
Let's understand - **How Validation Works in This API?**

**1. Validation Rules Defined in Model** \
In `User.java`, validation is applied directly on fields:
```java
@NotNull(message = "Name cannot be null")
@Size(min = 3, max = 10, message = "Name must be between 3 and 10 characters")
private String name;

@NotNull(message = "Email cannot be null")
@Email(message = "Invalid email format")
private String email;
```

**This means:**
- `name` must be present and between `3–10` characters
- `email` must be present and in valid format

---


**2. Validation Triggered in Controller**
```java
public ResponseEntity addUser(@Valid @RequestBody User user)
```
**`@Valid`** is the key here.

It tells Spring Boot: \
**“Before executing this method, validate the incoming request body.”**

---

**What Happens Internally** \
When a request is sent:

**Case 1: Valid Input**
```json
{
 "id": 1,
 "name": "Alice",
 "email": "alice@gmail.com"
}
```

**Flow:**
1. Request reaches controller
2. `@Valid` checks all rules
3. All validations pass 
4. Method executes
5. Data is stored
6. Response returned through:
```java
ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(user)
```
**Final Result:**
- 201 CREATED
- User saved successfully

---

**Case 2: Invalid Input**
```json
{
 "id": 2,
 "name": "Al",
 "email": "alice@gmail.com"
}
```
**Flow:**
1. Request reaches controller
2. `@Valid` starts validation
3. Rules fail 
4. Method is NOT executed
5. Spring automatically returns error

**Final Result:**
- 400 BAD REQUEST
- Error messages returned in terminal- [Name must be between 3 and 10 characters]

---


**Case 3: Invalid Email**
```json
{
 "id": 3,
 "name": "John",
 "email": "wrong-email"
}
```
**Flow:**
1. Request reaches controller
2. `@NotNull` starts validation
3. Rules fail 
4. Method is NOT executed
5. Spring automatically returns error

**Final Result:**
- 400 BAD REQUEST
- Error messages returned in terminal- [Invalid email format]


---

**Case 4: Missing Fields**
```json
{
 "id": 4
}
```
**Flow:**
1. Request reaches controller
2. `@Valid` starts validation
3. Rules fail 
4. Method is NOT executed
5. Spring automatically returns error

**Final Result:**
- 400 BAD REQUEST
- Error messages returned in terminal- \
[Email cannot be null] \
[Name cannot be null]

practiceProblems.title: Practice - Product API with Input Validation
practiceProblems.description:
You are required to complete the given template code for a Product Management API using Spring Boot that follows given requirements. \
This API should allow users to add products and view all products, **while ensuring that the input data is properly validated**.

---

**Instructions:**
1. **Complete your code** first.
2. Click on **"Run"** to **start the server** and make sure it runs correctly.
3. If you **make any changes** to the code after running, you must **run the server again**.
4. Only after running the server with the **latest changes**, your submission will reflect the updated solution.
5. **Do not submit** if the server is not running; otherwise, your solution will **fail**.




---

**Requirements**

**1. Create Product (POST /product)** \
Accept product details in JSON format and store them. \
Each product should contain:
- id (integer)
- name (string)
- brand (string)
- supplierEmail (string)


**2. Validation Rules**

You must apply the following validations:
- `name` \
Must not be null \
Length must be between 3 and 15 characters 
- `brand` \
Must not be null \
Minimum length should be 2 characters
- `supplierEmail` \
Must not be null \
Must be a valid email format

**3. Validation Behavior** \
If the input is **valid** → return **201 CREATED** \
If any validation **fails** → return **400 BAD REQUEST**

**4. Get All Products (GET /products)** \
Return the list of all stored products \
Response should have **200 OK*

---


**Example Request**

pages.title: Finder Methods in Spring Data JPA
pages.content:
Till now, you have used JpaRepository to perform basic operations like:
- `save()` → Create
- `findAll()` → Read
- `findById()` → Read by ID
- `delete()` → Delete

**Limitation** \
What if you want to:
- Find products by name
- Find users by email
- Get products with price greater than a value

**These cannot be done using only built-in methods**.

---

**Solution: Finder Methods** \
Spring Data JPA allows you to create custom queries just by writing method names.
- No SQL required
- No manual query writing


**How it works** \
You define a method in the repository like:
```JAVA
List findByName(String name);
```
Spring automatically understands:
- `findBy` → fetch data
- `Name` → filter field

**Example**
- findByName(String name)
- findByBrand(String brand)
- findByPriceGreaterThan(double price)

These methods are automatically converted into database queries.

---

**Why this is powerful**
- No need to write SQL
- Very easy to use
- Saves development time
- Widely used in real-world projects

Click on **"NEXT"** to see how to use Finder Methods used in a real API

practiceProblems.title: Demo - Finder Methods in Product API
practiceProblems.description:
Run the code, API tester will get open.
Go to POST endpoint and add below data :
```json
{
 "id": 1,
 "name": "Laptop",
 "brand": "Dell",
 "supplierEmail": "test@gmail.com"
}
```

Then test GET Requests using:
```sss
GET /products
GET /products/name/Laptop
GET /products/brand/Dell
```
Observe the Response data

As you can see in this API, we are retrieving products not just by ID, but based on **specific fields like name and brand**. \
These methods used to search/filter data are called Finder Methods.

---'

**Where Finder Methods are written** \
Look at your `ProductRepository`:
```java
public List findByName(String name) {
 return products.stream()
 .filter(p -> p.getName().equalsIgnoreCase(name))
 .collect(Collectors.toList());
}

public List findByBrand(String brand) {
 return products.stream()
 .filter(p -> p.getBrand().equalsIgnoreCase(brand))
 .collect(Collectors.toList());
}
```
**Here:**
- `findByName()` → finds products by name
- `findByBrand()` → finds products by brand

These are your custom finder methods

---

**How it works internally**

**When a request comes like:**
```sss
GET /products/name/Laptop
```
**Step-by-step flow:** 
1. Controller receives request
2. Calls service:
```java
service.getByName(name)
```
3. Service calls repository:
```java
repository.findByName(name)
```
4. Repository filters data using:
```java
stream().filter(...)
```
5. Matching products are returned

---

**Controller usage**
```java
@GetMapping("/products/name/{name}")
public ResponseEntity> getByName(@PathVariable String name) {
 return ResponseEntity.ok(service.getByName(name));
}
```
**Same for brand:**
```java
@GetMapping("/products/brand/{brand}")
```


---

**Key Understanding** \
Finder methods are used to:
- Search data
- Filter data
- Retrieve specific records

practiceProblems.title: Exclusive Club Registration Portal Project
practiceProblems.description:
**Hey Coders!** Welcome to the **Exclusive Club Registration Portal Project** 

In this project, you will build a **Spring Boot Backend** to manage the VIP roster of an elite club. When dealing with exclusive memberships, data quality is paramount. You cannot afford to have duplicate members, incomplete names, or permanently lost records.

Your **task** is to complete the backend logic to enforce strict data validation, prevent duplicate email registrations, and implement a professional "Soft Delete" mechanism so that no data is ever truly lost.

---

**Project Structure** \
You are given **5 Java files** representing a **Layered Architecture**:
 - **Entities (The Data Model):**
 - `Member.java` → Represents the club member's database record.
 - **DTOs (Data Transfer Objects):**
 - `MemberDTO.java` → Represents the incoming data from the user. Acts as a shield to validate input before it hits your core logic.
 - **Repositories (The Data Access Layer):**
 - `MemberRepository.java` → Interface that handles saving, retrieving, and executing custom SQL/JPQL queries.
 - **Service (The Business Logic):**
 - `MemberService.java` → Contains the **logic** to check for duplicates, save members, and process soft deletions.
 - **Controller (The API Layer):**
 - `MemberController.java` → Handles web requests, catches validation errors, and returns the appropriate HTTP status codes.

**Project Dependencies** \
To build this backend, your project is pre-configured with the following tools:
- **Spring Web:** For building RESTful API endpoints and handling HTTP requests.
- **Spring Data JPA:** For interacting with the database using Java objects instead of SQL.
- **H2 Database:** An in-memory database that stores your data while the app is running.
- **Spring Boot Validation:** To easily enforce rules on incoming data (like `@Email`).
- **Lombok:** A library that automatically generates boilerplate code like Getters, Setters, and Constructors.

---

**Important Rules**
- Do **NOT** change class names
- Do **NOT** change method names
- Complete the sections marked with **TODO**
- The testing system relies on the existing structure

**The Logic: Validation & Soft Deletion** \
This project focuses on **Data Integrity** and **Lifecycle Management**.
1. **Strict Validation:** A user cannot join with a blank name, a name shorter than 3 characters, or a fake email format. Your system must catch these before attempting to save to the database.
2. **Duplicate Prevention:** If an email is already in the database, the system must reject the registration.
3. **The "Soft Delete" Concept:** In real-world applications, we rarely use the SQL `DELETE` command. If a member leaves the club, we simply flip a boolean flag (`isDeleted = true`). This hides them from the active list but keeps their data safe for audits.

---

**Database Access (H2 Console)** \
If you want to visually check your tables and run SQL queries manually:
1. Run the file named `consoleViewer.js` and paste the CodeChef browser URL. For more details, refer to the project demonstration video.
 - Command to run the file:
 ```default
 node consoleViewer.js
 ```
2. Copy the URL printed in the output.
3. Paste it into your browser to access the H2 Console.
4. Write this JDBC URL `"jdbc:h2:mem:clubdb"` and click **Connect** to see your live data tables (for more details, check `application.properties` file).

---

**Your Task:**
1. **Complete the Entities**
- **File:** `entity/Member.java`
 - **Annotations:** Mark this class as a JPA Entity and map it to a table named `"members"`.
 - **Primary Key:** Configure the `id` field to be the Primary Key and set it to **Auto-Increment** using the `IDENTITY` strategy.
 - **Constructors:** Create a constructor that strictly takes name and email as parameters.
 - *Why do we need this?* Because the `id` is auto-generated by the database, and the `isDeleted` flag already defaults to `false`. When your Service layer converts the incoming DTO into a real Entity to save to the database, it only needs to provide the name and email!
 - **Getters & Setters:** Generate these for all fields (manually or using Lombok annotations) so other classes can access the data. \
**Docs:** Guide to JPA Entities | Lombok @Getter & @Setter | @Id and @GeneratedValue

2. **Configure the DTO Validation** \
 **File:** `dto/MemberDTO.java`
 - **Name Rules:**
 - Apply the correct validation annotation to ensure the name is actually provided (it cannot be null, and it cannot be just empty white spaces) using the custom message: (message = `"Name cannot be empty"`)
 - Add a second annotation to enforce that the string length is at least 3, using the custom message: (message = `"Name must be at least 3 characters"`).
 - **Email Rules:**
 - Apply a validation annotation to ensure the email field is not left blank, using the custom message: (message = `"Email is required"`)
 - Use the specific Spring annotation that verifies the string is formatted like a real email address, using the custom message: (message = `"Invalid email format"`).
 - **Getters & Setters:** Write the getters and setters for both fields. \
**Docs:** Spring Boot Validation Basics

3. **Build the Repository & Custom Queries** \
 **File:** `repository/MemberRepository.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this interface as a Repository.
 - **Inheritance:** Extend the standard `JpaRepository` interface.
 - **Generics:** You must specify two things for each repository:
 1. The **Entity Type** it manages (e.g., `Member`).
 2. The **Data Type** of that Entity's Primary Key.
 - **Derived Query:** Create a method named `findByEmail` that returns an `Optional`.
 - **Custom JPQL:** Use the `@Query` annotation to write a custom JPQL query that selects all members where `isDeleted` is false. \
**Docs:** Spring Data JPA Custom Queries | Java Optional Class | @Repository Annotation | JpaRepository Interface

4. **Build the Service** \
 **File:** `service/MemberService.java`
 - **Annotation:** Add the correct Spring annotation to mark this class as a Service.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Define the repository as `private final` field and initialize them via **Constructor Injection**.
 - **Registration Logic:** Call your derived query to check if the email exists. If `isPresent()` is true, throw a `RuntimeException` with the exact message `"Email already registered!"`.
 - **Soft Delete Logic:** Find the member by ID. If not present, throw an error. If present, use the setter to change `isDeleted` to `true`, then save the member back to the repository.
 - **Fetch Active Members:** Return the results of your custom JPQL query. \
**Docs:** @Service Annotation | Constructor Dependency Injection | Spring Data CrudRepository Methods (save, findById)

5. **Define the API Endpoints** \
 **File:** `controller/MemberController.java`
 - **Class Configuration:** Annotate the class to make it a **REST Controller** and define the base URL path as `"/api"`.
 - **Dependency Injection:** Inject the `MemberService` using the constructor.
 - **Endpoint 1:** Register (**POST** `/register`)
 - Use `@Valid` and `@RequestBody` together to validate and bind the incoming JSON to the `MemberDTO`.
 - Check `result.hasErrors()`. If true, return a `BAD_REQUEST` (400) status (Code provided).
 - If the service throws an exception (like a duplicate email), catch it and return a `BAD_REQUEST` (400) status.
 - **Endpoint 2:** Delete (**DELETE** `/{id}`)
 - Use the correct annotation to extract the `id` directly from the URL path so it can be passed into your method.
 - Attempt to soft-delete the member using your service. If the service throws an exception because the member doesn't exist, catch it and return an HTTP status indicating the resource was not found (404).
 - **Endpoint 3:** View Active (**GET** `/`)
 - Fetch the list of active members from your service and wrap the result in a response entity that signifies a successful 200 OK HTTP status. \
**Docs:** @RestController Annotation | ResponseEntity | Overview of @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @DeleteMapping | Spring @PathVariable | @RequestBody Annotation

---

**Expected Behaviour:** \
Before submitting the project, ensure the **backend server is running**. If you make any changes to the code, you must **restart the server** for those changes to take effect.
